text:
Examine this sequence of commands:

```text
crsctl disable crs
crsctl stop cluster -all
crsctl start cluster -all
```

The cluster consists of nodes HOST01, HOST02, HOST03 and HOST04, and the clusterware is running on all four nodes.

Which three statements are true about the result of the root user running these commands on HOST01? (Choose three.)

options.text: The Oracle Clusterware stack is stopped on all nodes.
The Oracle Clusterware stack is prevented from being automatically started on HOST01.
The Oracle Clusterware stack is prevented from being automatically started on all nodes.
The Oracle Clusterware stack is stopped on all nodes except HOST01.
The Oracle Clusterware stack is started on all nodes except HOST01.
The Oracle Clusterware stack is started on all nodes.

explanation:
The key is A, B and F. Read the commands in order, and distinguish a boot-time setting from an immediate start or stop operation. The answer about stopping describes the intermediate result; it does not mean that the stack remains stopped after the final command.

A is correct: `crsctl stop cluster -all` requests a cluster-wide stop, including HOST01. The cluster-aware operation coordinates the stop across member nodes. B is correct: `crsctl disable crs` changes the local Oracle High Availability Services autostart setting on HOST01. It neither propagates to the other three nodes nor immediately stops the running stack. F is correct: the subsequent `crsctl start cluster -all` starts Clusterware across the nodes. The stop-cluster operation leaves the lower-level infrastructure needed for cluster-aware remote operations available.

C is false because disable-crs has local scope. D is false because `-all` does not exclude the node issuing the command. E is false because disabling automatic startup on HOST01 is not a prohibition against an explicit start request while its OHASD remains available.

For a practical check, examine the boot setting separately from current resource state:
```text
crsctl config crs
crsctl check cluster -all
crsctl status resource -t
```
After this sequence, HOST01 can have a running stack while its next-boot autostart setting is disabled. If OHASD itself is stopped or the host is rebooted with autostart disabled, the administrator must start it locally with `crsctl start crs` before cluster-aware remote operations can manage that node. The key distinction is persistent autostart configuration versus the current running state.

sources.title: CRSCTL reference: disable crs, start/stop cluster

mnemonic.anchor: Read the commands in order, and distinguish a boot-time setting from an immediate start or stop operation.

text: Which two statements are true concerning diagnostic components and requirements of Oracle 19c Clusterware? (Choose two.)

options.text: The clusterware log files are stored inside the Grid Infrastructure Management Repository database used by the cluster health monitor (CHM).
The diagcollection.pl script must be run from the Grid home directory as the grid infrastructure owner.
There is one ologgerd service for the cluster health monitor (CHM) on each cluster node regardless of cluster size.
The oclumon utility may be used to get and set parameters for the cluster health monitor (CHM ) repository.
There is one osysmond service for the cluster health monitor (CHM) on each cluster node regardless of cluster size.

explanation:
The key is D and E. Cluster Health Monitor collects operating-system measurements; it is not a replacement location for all Clusterware diagnostic log files. Separate the collection daemon on every node from the logger and repository infrastructure that receives those measurements.

D is correct because `oclumon manage` can inspect CHM configuration and repository information and change supported repository settings. The precise effect of an option matters: current 19c AHF documentation describes `changeretentiontime` as a capacity check, whereas `changerepossize` changes the repository space limit. Therefore, do not assume every command containing the word retention directly changes a retention policy.

E is correct: the System Monitor Service, `osysmond`, runs on each cluster node and gathers the local operating-system metrics sent to the Cluster Logger Service. C confuses the node-local collectors with `ologgerd`; a separate logger on every node is not a universal requirement independent of cluster size and deployment.

A is false because Clusterware alert and trace files are stored in diagnostic locations on disk. The GIMR can hold management and diagnostic data, but saying all Clusterware logs are stored inside that database is incorrect. B is false because Oracle documents running `diagcollection.pl` as root from `Grid_home/bin`, not as the Grid Infrastructure software owner from the home directory itself.

Useful read-only investigation commands include:
```text
oclumon manage -get alllogger -details
oclumon manage -get repsize
```
When investigating an incident, collect both the Clusterware trace/alert evidence and the relevant CHM time window. A healthy `osysmond` process proves collection is running on that node; it does not by itself establish that every downstream repository or logger component is healthy.

mnemonic.anchor: Cluster Health Monitor collects operating-system measurements; it is not a replacement location for all Clusterware diagnostic log files.

text: Which statement is true about Oracle Database 19c SGA Management?

options.text: Oracle RAC Resource Management only allows assignment of the SGA during instance startup.
Oracle RAC Resource Management requires the same SGA value for all the instances of a RAC database which is configured during database startup only.
Oracle RAC Resource Runtime Management allows for automatic and runtime adjustment of the SGA.
Oracle RAC Resource Management only allows assignment of the SGA during database startup.

explanation:
C is correct. Oracle RAC Resource Runtime Management, introduced in the 19c release family, allows resources such as SGA capacity to be adjusted during database operation instead of treating all allocations as fixed for the life of an instance. Oracle specifically describes SGA growth during runtime and automatic runtime resource adjustment beginning with 19.3.

A and D are false because they restrict SGA assignment to instance or database startup. Some memory settings do require a restart, but that does not make all SGA sizing static. For example, `SGA_MAX_SIZE` establishes a startup ceiling, whereas `SGA_TARGET` can be changed dynamically within the supported configuration and available capacity. B adds another incorrect restriction: RAC instances are not universally required to have identical SGA sizes. Instance-specific workload and hardware can justify different settings, even where consistent settings simplify administration.

Automatic Shared Memory Management distributes the SGA target among eligible components. Automatic Memory Management can additionally coordinate SGA and PGA targets where supported and configured. These database memory mechanisms should not be confused with a guarantee that every memory request can be satisfied immediately: operating-system memory, configured maxima, platform restrictions and workload still matter.

For example, inspect memory and then make an explicitly scoped change in a suitable lab:
```sql
SELECT inst_id, name, value
FROM gv$parameter
WHERE name IN ('sga_target','sga_max_size','memory_target');

ALTER SYSTEM SET sga_target=4G SCOPE=BOTH SID='rac1';
```
The SID is illustrative and must match the real instance. Check component resize activity and operating-system memory afterward. The lesson is that runtime adjustability exists; it does not eliminate planning, per-instance configuration or the distinction between a dynamic target and a static upper bound.

mnemonic.anchor: Oracle specifically describes SGA growth during runtime and automatic runtime resource adjustment beginning with 19.3.

text:
Zero Downtime Patching uses Fleet Patching and Provisioning to patch Oracle Grid Infrastructure without bringing down Oracle RAC database instances.

Which three statements are true about Zero-Downtime Oracle Grid Infrastructure Patching? (Choose three.)

options.text: Zero Downtime Patching requires out-of-place patching of Oracle Grid Infrastructure 19c with Oracle RAC or Oracle RAC One Node databases of 19c or later releases and only the binaries in the Oracle Grid Infrastructure user space are patched.
When using Zero Downtime Patching, the root.sh script must be executed manually with -nodriverupdate option.
When using Zero Downtime Patching, Oracle Grid Infrastructure OS system software, kernel modules and system commands including ACFS, AFD, OLFS, and OKA are not updated.

Zero Downtime Patching requires in-place patching of Oracle Grid Infrastructure 19c with Oracle RAC or Oracle RAC One Node databases of 19c or later releases and only the binaries in the Oracle Grid Infrastructure user space are patched.
Zero Downtime Patching can be fully automated by selecting the option to automatically run the root.sh script.

explanation:
The key is A, C and E. Zero-downtime Grid Infrastructure patching updates eligible GI software while supported 19c-or-later RAC or RAC One Node database instances continue operating. This is a particular patching method, not a promise that every GI patch can be installed without any service interruption.

A is correct: the method uses a separate patched Grid home, so it is out-of-place. For the Fleet Patching and Provisioning method named in the question, Oracle documents support beginning with the appropriate 19.8 release update level. Other documented mechanisms, such as later `switchGridHome` workflows, have their own minimum RU requirements. D reverses the required out-of-place characteristic and is therefore false.

C is correct in operational effect: GI operating-system components such as ACFS, AFD, OLFS and OKA are not replaced in their active system locations during the zero-downtime phase. Updated copies may be present in the new Grid home, while the running OS drivers and tools continue at their previous level. A later maintenance operation is needed to install those updated system components.

E is correct because supported orchestration can automate privileged root-script execution using the configured execution method. B is false: manual execution of `root.sh -nodriverupdate` is not the mandatory workflow described for this feature.

In practice, record three things separately: the GI home inventory, the Clusterware state, and the active driver versions. For example:
```text
opatch lsinventory
crsctl query driver softwareversion -all
crsctl query driver activeversion -all
```
Use the OPatch executable from the relevant home. A difference between available and active driver levels can be expected after this method. Always follow the patch README and the exact FPP/RU procedure; listeners running from the Grid home can restart even while database instances remain available.

sources.title: GI home binaries versus operating-system drivers

mnemonic.anchor: Zero-downtime Grid Infrastructure patching updates eligible GI software while supported 19c-or-later RAC or RAC One Node database instances continue operating.

text: Which statement is true concerning the installation of an Oracle Grid Infrastructure 19c patchset and its status during the installation?

options.text: They can be applied in-place.
When performing rolling patches, the VIPs for the node being patched are relocated to another node.
Some Grid Infrastructure patchsets may not be installed in a rolling fashion.
When performing rolling patches, crsctl query crs softwareversion always displays the earliest version of the software running anywhere in the cluster.

explanation:
B is the intended answer: during normal rolling GI maintenance, the node VIP can be relocated to another eligible surviving node while the original node's Clusterware resources are taken down. This supports rapid notification of connection failures; it does not transfer existing database sessions or make the old instance continue executing.

However, the question is ambiguous as written because “patchset” mixes older upgrade terminology with 19c patch and release-update procedures. A cannot be rejected as a universal statement about every 19c patch: Oracle documents in-place OPatch/OPatchAuto workflows as well as out-of-place methods. For a traditional GI patch-set upgrade, a separate home is the relevant model. C is also too dependent on the actual patch: rolling eligibility is determined by patch metadata and the README, rather than by the blanket claim that any arbitrary patch is rolling-capable.

D is definitely false. `crsctl query crs softwareversion` reports software for a specified node or the local node. The cluster active version is a different concept, and can remain at the earlier level until a rolling upgrade completes. Confusing softwareversion with activeversion is the principal diagnostic trap.

A practical maintenance plan first identifies the exact patch type and whether it is rolling-installable. Then inspect resource placement and versions:
```text
crsctl status resource -t
crsctl query crs softwareversion
crsctl query crs activeversion
```
Retain B as the simulator's intended key, but do not treat this item as a uniquely proven single-answer question for all 19c maintenance scenarios. To make it rigorous, the stem would need to identify a particular rolling GI procedure or a specific patch README and clarify whether it means patch-set upgrade, release update or one-off patch.

sources.title: Supported maintenance tools and in-place capabilities

review_note: The generic term patchset leaves A/C dependent on the patch type and README; B is the intended rolling-maintenance answer, not a universal unique key.

mnemonic.anchor: This supports rapid notification of connection failures; it does not transfer existing database sessions or make the old instance continue executing.

text: Which three statements are true about the administration and use of policy sets in Oracle 19c Clusterware? (Choose three.)

options.text: All server pools in a cluster are controlled by the policy set, when user-defined policy management is used.
Clusterware administrators cannot directly modify the policy set when Quality of Service (QoS) Management is used.
A server pool can have different attributes defined for different policies in the policy set, when user-defined policy management is used.
A server pool can have the same attributes defined for different policies in the policy set, when user-defined policy management is used.
Servers in a server pool outside the control of the policy set are never affected by policy changes, when user-defined policy management is used.

explanation:
The defensible key is B, C and D. A policy set stores alternative configurations, and one policy is active at a time. Policies can change the capacity and placement constraints of the server pools they manage; they do not imply that every pool and every server in the cluster is permanently insulated from the rest of the allocation engine.

B is correct: when Oracle Database QoS Management controls the policies, the CRSCTL policy and policyset commands are disabled. Administrators manage the corresponding policy through QoS rather than maintaining a competing Clusterware policy set directly. Oracle explicitly warns that the two policy types cannot coexist.

C is correct because the same server pool can have different attributes in different policies. For instance, an OLTP pool can require three servers during business hours and one overnight. D is also correct: policies do not require every attribute of every pool to differ. Two policies may retain identical attributes for a pool while changing another pool or another requirement.

A is false because it overstates the scope of the selected policy set: membership and management are explicit, and not all pools have to be controlled in the same way. E is unsafe because “never affected” is absolute. Servers are physical capacity shared by the pool-allocation system; a policy transition can trigger reassignment and resource movement subject to pool constraints and priorities.

Inspect the complete policy configuration before activating changes:
```text
crsctl status policyset
crsctl status serverpool -p
crsctl status resource -t
```
Think through the difference between changing a pool's definition and changing which servers supply its capacity. A policy can preserve a particular pool's settings while other changes still affect server allocation. The original A/C/E key incorrectly treated “all” and “never” as guarantees.

sources.title: Cluster configuration policies, QoS restrictions and server allocation

mnemonic.anchor: A policy set stores alternative configurations, and one policy is active at a time.

text:
Disk group DGRP1 has these attributes:

1. Normal redundancy
2. Two failure groups FG1 and FG2 with two disks each
3. Compatibility settings set to 19.0

The FG1 failure group goes offline due to hardware failure.

Which two statements are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: New allocation units are mirrored in the FG2 failure group until FG1 is restored and the disk group resynchronized.
The redundancy is lowered until the FG1 failgroup is restored and the disk group resynchronized.
New allocation units are not mirrored but changes to allocation units are tracked in the FG2 failure group.
Transactions on database objects stored in tablespaces in the DGRP1 disk group fail.

explanation:
The key is B and C, provided the failure is temporary, FG1 remains an offline member, and the files have a surviving copy in FG2. Normal redundancy places mirrored extents in different failure groups. Two disks in FG2 do not become two independent failure groups simply because FG1 is unavailable.

B is correct: the data is accessible with reduced protection while one failure group's copies are unavailable. C is correct: ASM tracks extents modified while the disks are offline so that fast mirror resync can repair only changed regions when those disks return. With no other failure group available, new allocations cannot obtain the normal cross-failure-group mirrored protection until redundancy can be restored.

A is false because placing both copies inside FG2 would defeat the failure-group isolation that normal redundancy is designed to provide. D is false under the stated single-failure-group loss: database work can continue using surviving copies. It would become a different situation if another required copy were lost, the disk group dismounted, or unavailable disks were dropped and the remaining storage could not satisfy allocation requirements.

For a lab, inspect disk state, repair time and resynchronization progress:
```sql
SELECT name, state, mode_status, repair_timer
FROM v$asm_disk;
SELECT group_number, operation, state, sofar, est_work
FROM v$asm_operation;
```
Issue these from the ASM instance with appropriate privileges. Repair or restore connectivity before the offline-repair window expires; the relevant limit is a disk-group attribute, not a database transaction timeout. Fast mirror resync is efficient because ASM remembers what changed. It is not another mirror copy, and operating in this degraded state leaves the database exposed to an additional storage failure.

sources.title: ASM failure groups, offline disks and fast mirror resync
Offline disks, repair time and resynchronization

mnemonic.anchor: , provided the failure is temporary, FG1 remains an offline member, and the files have a surviving copy in FG2.

text:
You administer a RAC database that currently runs on a four-node cluster but which has three instances.

Which two statements are always true about redo logs for this RAC database? (Choose two.)

options.text: A thread of redo must be created before starting a fourth instance if a thread is not already available.
A thread of redo is automatically dropped when an instance is removed from a RAC database by using SRVCTL.
All the instances must have the same number of redo log groups and each group must have the same number of redo log members.
A redo log group added using ALTER DATABASE ADD LOGFILE without the INSTANCE clause is added to each instance.
A thread of redo must contain at least two log groups before it can be enabled.

explanation:
The intended key is A and E. A RAC instance writes its own redo thread; the number of cluster nodes does not itself create a usable thread for every possible instance. A fourth open instance needs an available enabled thread, and that thread must contain sufficient online log groups.

A is correct in the sense that the necessary thread must exist before the fourth instance can use it. Do not read this as an unconditional manual DBA step: for a policy-managed database using the supported Oracle Managed Files configuration, Oracle can create the thread and redo files automatically as instance capacity grows. E is correct because each redo thread needs at least two log groups so LGWR can switch from one group to another.

B is false: removing an instance from Clusterware management with SRVCTL does not in itself guarantee SQL-level removal of its redo thread and log groups. C confuses a recommendation for consistent configuration with an absolute requirement. Threads can have different numbers of groups, and group multiplexing need not be identical across every instance. D is false because one ADD LOGFILE operation does not duplicate a new group into every thread. Use an explicit THREAD clause when provisioning another thread.

For example, inspect the current allocation before adding capacity:
```sql
SELECT thread#, status, enabled, instance FROM v$thread;
SELECT thread#, group#, members, status FROM v$log
ORDER BY thread#, group#;
```
In a manually managed example, adding two groups to thread 4 and enabling that thread are distinct steps. Redo files must also be accessible to surviving instances for recovery. The key distinction is a node, an instance, a redo thread, a log group and a multiplexed log member: these are related objects, but they are not interchangeable counts.

sources.title: Online redo threads per RAC instance
RAC 19c architecture: redo and automatic thread creation

mnemonic.anchor: A RAC instance writes its own redo thread; the number of cluster nodes does not itself create a usable thread for every possible instance.

text: Which two steps must always be performed to delete node host04 from an Oracle 19c Clusterware cluster that does not use Grid Naming Service (GNS)? (Choose two.)

options.text: Run the crsctl unpin css - host04 command as root on host01, or on either host02 or host03.
Run the crsctl delete node -n host04 command as root on host04.
Run the crsctl delete node -n host04 command as root on host01, or on either host02 or host03.
Run the crsct1 unpin css - host04 command as root on host04.
Run the rootcrs.pl -deconfig -force command as root on host04.
Run the rootcrs.pl -deconfig -force command as root on host01, or on either host02 or host03.

explanation:
C and E describe the intended separation of local deconfiguration and cluster membership deletion. The departing node must stop participating in Clusterware, while a surviving node removes its membership record. Unpinning is conditional: it is needed only if the node is pinned, so it cannot be an “always” requirement.

C is correct: run `crsctl delete node -n host04` as root from a node that is remaining in the cluster. B puts that membership-deletion command on the node being deleted, contrary to the documented surviving-node procedure. E describes deconfiguring the departing node; F applies that disruptive operation to a healthy surviving node instead.

There is a version and wording defect. The 19c Linux/UNIX procedure documents `rootcrs.sh`, not the older `rootcrs.pl` spelling shown in E/F. Also, for a local Grid home, Oracle documents `deinstall -local`; explicit `rootcrs.sh -deconfig -force` is shown for the shared-home branch. Consequently, literal E is not a universal stand-alone command that every 19c removal must execute manually. A and D are additionally malformed and make conditional unpinning unconditional.

The modern shared-home conceptual sequence includes:
```text
# On the departing node, following all documented prerequisites:
Grid_home/crs/install/rootcrs.sh -deconfig -force
# On a surviving node:
crsctl delete node -n host04
```
This is an explanatory example, not a complete removal runbook: database instances, home inventory, services and a possible residual VIP also require attention. Verify the result using CVU and cluster membership tools. Retain CE as the bank's intended key, but learn the actual 19c workflow and identify the home type before issuing deconfiguration commands.

sources.title: 19c node deletion: local/shared-home procedures and surviving-node deletion

review_note: E uses legacy rootcrs.pl and says always despite local-home/shared-home alternatives. CE is the intended conceptual key; follow rootcrs.sh/deinstall guidance for 19c.

keywords: delete node -n host04 command as root on host01
rootcrs.pl -deconfig -force command as root on host04
mnemonic.anchor: C and E describe the intended separation of local deconfiguration and cluster membership deletion.

text: Which three statements are true about services and load balancing for Oracle 19c clients connecting to Oracle 19c RAC database instances? (Choose three.)

options.text: Services support the balancing of client connections across RAC database instances.
In server-side load balancing, node listener redirects the client to another node listener for connection to an instance.
Load balancing can be done by the client or the listener, but not both, for any one connection request.
Client-side connect-time load balancing can balance connection requests across SCAN listeners.
Load balancing can be done by the client, the listener, or both, for any one connection request.

explanation:
The key is A, D and E. There are two decisions during a typical connection: the client chooses a listener address, and the SCAN listener chooses an instance that offers the requested service. These decisions operate at different stages, so they can both be used for one connection attempt.

A is correct because a database service identifies eligible instances and carries connection and runtime load-balancing goals. D is correct because client-side address selection can distribute initial requests across SCAN listeners. A modern SCAN-aware client obtains the SCAN addresses through name resolution; older clients may require an explicit address list. E is correct: Oracle recommends using both client-side and server-side connection load balancing for RAC.

B is false in the stated SCAN architecture. The SCAN listener redirects a request to the local listener of an appropriate instance; it is not a general node-listener-to-another-node-listener chain. C is the opposite of E and incorrectly makes the two balancing stages mutually exclusive.

A useful practical check is to inspect the service configuration and listener registration:
```text
srvctl config service -db CDB1 -service orders
lsnrctl services LISTENER_SCAN1
```
Replace names with the actual resources. A service with the desired connection goal is useful only if the instances offering it are properly registered. Also distinguish connection-time balancing from runtime balancing: existing physical connections are not redistributed simply because another instance becomes less busy. Supported connection pools can consume Load Balancing Advisory events and select connections for individual work requests, whereas a basic client that opens one long-lived connection only benefits from the initial placement decision.

The trap is treating SCAN as a replacement for all other load-balancing behavior. It provides a stable entry name and listener selection/redirect path; service placement and client capabilities still determine the actual behavior.

sources.title: Connection load balancing, SCAN and runtime advisory

mnemonic.anchor: These decisions operate at different stages, so they can both be used for one connection attempt.

text: Which three statements are true regarding multitenant architecture for RAC databases? (Choose three.)

options.text: One UNDO tablespace for each PDB is required.
PDBs can have local temporary tablespaces.
You can open one, several, or all PDBs on one, several, or all CDB instances.
It requires the CDB to use shared UNDO management.
One UNDO tablespace for each instance is required.
PDBs must use shared Temporary tablespace.

explanation:
The intended key is B, C and E. RAC and multitenant address different dimensions: instances provide compute and shared database access, while containers provide database isolation. A PDB need not be open in every instance simply because the CDB has several running instances.

B is correct: local temporary tablespaces are supported, and a PDB can have its own temporary-space configuration. F incorrectly makes a shared temporary tablespace mandatory. C is correct because an administrator can open a PDB on selected CDB instances; opening it on one instance does not require opening it everywhere.

E expresses the RAC rule that simultaneous writers on different instances require separate active undo tablespaces. The important 19c qualification is undo mode. In shared undo mode, the CDB has an active undo tablespace for each instance. In local undo mode, each container needs its own active undo tablespace for every instance in which that container is open. Therefore E must not be interpreted as exactly one undo tablespace per entire instance regardless of its PDBs.

A is not an unconditional description of RAC CDBs: shared undo mode does not require a separate PDB undo tablespace, and local undo requires an instance dimension as well. D is false because RAC does not require shared undo; local undo is supported and enables important PDB operations.

Use these checks from the root:
```sql
SELECT property_value FROM database_properties
WHERE property_name='LOCAL_UNDO_ENABLED';
SELECT inst_id, name, open_mode FROM gv$pdbs
ORDER BY name, inst_id;
```
Before changing a PDB open state, consider where its application service is placed. Service availability, container open state, local undo and temporary storage are related requirements; none should be inferred solely from the number of running CDB instances.

sources.title: CDB undo modes and per-instance local undo

mnemonic.anchor: RAC and multitenant address different dimensions: instances provide compute and shared database access, while containers provide database isolation.

text:
Secure Cluster Communication protects the cluster interconnect from common security threats when used together with Single Network Support. Secure Cluster Communication includes message digest mechanisms, protection against fuzzing, and uses Transport Layer Security (TLS) to provide privacy and data integrity between the cluster members.

Which statement is true about securing cluster interconnect communication?

options.text: Security for the cluster interconnect is invoked automatically as part of a new Oracle Grid Infrastructure 19c deployment or an upgrade to Oracle Grid Infrastructure 19c and Database administrators or cluster administrators do not need to make any configuration changes for this feature.

Security for the cluster interconnect is invoked automatically as part of a new Oracle Grid Infrastructure 19c deployment or an upgrade to Oracle Grid Infrastructure 19c using an auto-generated encryption key that is stored locally on each node of the cluster in an Oracle Wallet and Database administrators or cluster administrators must provide a valid path for the Wallet file.

Security for the cluster interconnect is invoked by auto-generated server certificates that will be assigned to each cluster node as part of a new Oracle Grid Infrastructure 19c deployment or an upgrade to Oracle Grid Infrastructure 19c.

Database administrators or cluster administrators must provide an encryption key during new Oracle Grid Infrastructure 19c deployment or an upgrade to Oracle Grid Infrastructure 19c to secure the interconnect communication.

Database administrators or cluster administrators must provide a valid server certificate and an Oracle Wallet for each node during new Oracle Grid Infrastructure 19c deployment or an upgrade to Oracle Grid Infrastructure 19c to secure the interconnect communication.

explanation:
A is correct. Oracle lists Secure Cluster Communication as a 19c feature that is invoked automatically for a new Grid Infrastructure deployment or an upgrade to 19c. The administrator does not have to supply a wallet location, manually import certificates or create an encryption key to activate this built-in protection.

The feature adds protection for cluster-member communication through mechanisms including message digests, resistance to malformed-message attacks and TLS for privacy and integrity. This concerns protected internal communication in the supported Clusterware network configuration. It should not be interpreted as automatically encrypting every application connection to a database listener or every network protocol running on the hosts.

B is false because it adds a mandatory administrator-provided wallet path. C is not the documented administrative behavior: the question's valid claim is automatic activation without the asserted per-node certificate-assignment procedure. D and E explicitly require the administrator to provide keys, certificates or wallets during deployment, contradicting Oracle's description.

A practical example is a newly installed 19c cluster using its supported private interconnect configuration. You validate cluster health and private-network classification rather than inventing wallet provisioning steps:
```text
oifcfg getif
crsctl check cluster -all
```
Network classification and connectivity still have to satisfy installation requirements. For database client/server encryption, independently configure and validate the appropriate Oracle Net TLS or native-network-encryption settings for the application's requirements.

The exam distinction is automatic internal security versus a customer-managed certificate deployment. Automatically enabled does not mean all security administration disappears: patching, network isolation, endpoint permissions and supported cipher configuration remain operational responsibilities. It means this particular Clusterware feature does not require the manual initialization steps proposed in the incorrect options.

mnemonic.anchor: Oracle lists Secure Cluster Communication as a 19c feature that is invoked automatically for a new Grid Infrastructure deployment or an upgrade to 19c.

text: Which two statements are true about V$ASM_* views in a clustered environment? (Choose two.)

options.text: They exist in both ASM and RDBMS instances, but they can display different outputs depending on the instance type.
Their names can be seen in v$fixed_table when connected to an instance of any type that is started.
Their names can be seen in dict when connected to an ASM instance.
gv$asm_attribute can be used to display the ASM_POWER_LIMIT attribute of all ASM instances in the cluster.
They exist in both ASM and RDBMS instances, and display the same output.

explanation:
The key is A and B. Dynamic performance views are fixed-instance views, and their availability does not mean they expose the same information from every instance type. An ASM instance manages disk groups; a database instance is a client of ASM and sees the subset relevant to its own open ASM files.

A is correct. For example, `V$ASM_CLIENT` in ASM identifies database clients using its disk groups, while the database-side view reports information about the ASM connection used by that database. B is correct because `V$FIXED_TABLE` enumerates fixed dynamic-performance views available in a started instance. You do not need a normal database data dictionary just to discover those fixed views.

C is false: `DICT`/`DICTIONARY` belongs to the database data dictionary model; it is not the appropriate catalogue for ASM's fixed views. D is false because `ASM_POWER_LIMIT` is an ASM instance initialization parameter. `GV$ASM_ATTRIBUTE` exposes disk-group attributes such as compatibility and repair-related settings, not that initialization parameter. E is false because the same view name does not guarantee the same rows or interpretation in ASM and RDBMS instances.

The following demonstrates the distinction:
```sql
SELECT name FROM v$fixed_table
WHERE name LIKE 'V$ASM%';

SELECT inst_id, value FROM gv$parameter
WHERE name='asm_power_limit';
```
Run the second query while connected to the ASM instance with appropriate administrative privileges. To inspect a disk-group attribute, query `V$ASM_ATTRIBUTE` instead, filtering by its actual attribute name. The crucial question is where the setting belongs: instance parameters control an ASM instance, whereas disk-group attributes describe an individual storage group and can differ between groups mounted by the same instance.

text:
Examine this command executed on the first node of a four-node cluster:

```text
$ <DATABASE_ORACLE_HOME>/OPatch/opatch apply 33575673
```

What does this command do?

options.text: It applies a patch to one ORACLE_HOME only on the first cluster node.
It applies a patch to one database ORACLE_HOME on all cluster nodes.
It applies a patch to all database ORACLE_HOMEs with the same release only on the first cluster node.
It applies a patch to all ORACLE_HOMEs with the same release only on the first cluster node.
It applies a patch to all database ORACLE_HOMEs with the same release on all cluster nodes.

explanation:
A is the intended local-home answer, but the abbreviated command is insufficient to prove the complete node scope. OPatch operates on a selected Oracle home, and the patch argument names the patch directory. It does not discover and patch every database home that happens to have the same release number.

C, D and E are false because they multiply the operation across unrelated Oracle homes. A home contains a particular installation and inventory; matching release numbers do not make other homes targets. B versus A requires more care than the original explanation allowed. OPatch has historically supported RAC-aware propagation options, and Oracle's OPatch command reference documents `-local` specifically as preventing propagation and inventory updates to remote nodes. The command in the question lacks that explicit option and gives no patch README, inventory topology, OPatch version or interactive responses.

In the usual modern manual per-node patch workflow, the expected interpretation is the local database home on the first node. However, an explanation that plain `opatch apply` is strictly local under every possible clustered configuration overstates the evidence. Neither the numerical patch identifier nor the executable's path supplies the missing cluster-installation details.

A useful non-installing investigation is:
```text
DATABASE_ORACLE_HOME/OPatch/opatch version
DATABASE_ORACLE_HOME/OPatch/opatch apply -help
DATABASE_ORACLE_HOME/OPatch/opatch lsinventory -detail
```
Then read the actual patch README. If the approved plan requires a strictly local operation, use the documented local option where appropriate to that patch procedure. Also distinguish binary patching from database SQL patching: applying binaries to a home does not by itself demonstrate that `datapatch` has completed for every database using it. This item should remain marked ambiguous until its intended patch and OPatch context are specified.

text: Which two tasks must be performed before launching the Oracle universal installer to install Oracle Database Software for RAC? (Choose two.)

options.text: SSH user equivalence for the Oracle software owner must be configured on all cluster nodes where the Database software will be installed.
Grid Infrastructure must be installed on all cluster nodes.
The Clusterware stack must be up on all cluster nodes.
The Clusterware stack must be up on all cluster nodes where the Database software will be installed.
SSH user equivalence for the Oracle software owner must be configured on all cluster nodes.
Grid Infrastructure must be installed on all cluster nodes where the Database software will be installed.

explanation:
The key is D and F. A RAC database software installation depends on a working Grid Infrastructure layer on the nodes selected for that database home. The question asks about prerequisites before launching the database installer, so distinguish what must already exist from configuration that the installer can help create.

D is correct because the Clusterware stack must be running on the nodes on which RAC database software will be installed. F is correct because those selected nodes must already have the required Grid Infrastructure installation. A database software installation does not itself create the underlying cluster that it is supposed to discover and use.

A is not an obligatory pre-launch task: passwordless SSH connectivity for the software owner is required for distributed installation work, but Oracle allows the installer to configure it. It is therefore wrong to insist it must always be configured manually before the installer is launched. E adds an overbroad all-cluster-nodes requirement to the same timing error. B and C likewise say all cluster nodes, whereas the particular RAC software home can be installed on a chosen subset of eligible nodes.

Before opening OUI, verify the selected installation nodes and the GI stack:
```text
olsnodes
crsctl check cluster -all
```
Confirm software-owner accounts, groups, permissions and storage requirements as well. If the cluster has four nodes but the new RAC database home is initially installed on two, the database installer must be able to operate on those two selected nodes. There is no requirement in this question to install that database home on the other two merely because they belong to the cluster.

The exam trap is the word “before.” A requirement that must be satisfied by the time remote installation proceeds is not necessarily a task that must have been completed before the installer starts. Oracle's SSH setup support makes that distinction decisive here.

text: Which two statements are true concerning Oracle 19c Clusterware-managed application VIPs? (Choose two.)

options.text: An application VIP is created on the default network by the appvipcfg utility.
Application VIPs do not fail over to surviving cluster nodes when the node hosting the VIP fails.
If an application sends messages to be displayed and sets the DISPLAY variable, then an application VIP is required.
An application VIP can be created with the crsctl utility.
An application VIP is created on the interconnect network by the crsctl utility.

explanation:
The key is A and D. An application VIP gives clients a stable network endpoint for a Clusterware-managed application. The resource can move to another eligible node when its hosting node fails, following its placement and dependency configuration.

A is correct for the default public-network case: `appvipcfg` creates an application VIP associated with network 1, whose Clusterware network resource is normally `ora.net1.network`. The utility requires the network number explicitly. It can also be used with a configured non-default public network, so A should not be read as saying application VIPs are restricted forever to network 1.

D is correct because an application VIP is a Clusterware resource and can be registered through CRSCTL with a suitable resource type and attributes. Oracle recommends the application-VIP utility for the common case because it supplies the appropriate resource model. B is false: lack of failover would defeat a primary reason for using a managed application VIP. C is unrelated; the DISPLAY environment variable controls X display selection, not whether an application needs a failover IP address. E is false because the private interconnect is not the normal public client endpoint for an application VIP.

An illustrative creation and inspection sequence is:
```text
appvipcfg create -network=1 -ip=192.0.2.40 -vipname=appvip -user=oracle
crsctl status resource appvip -p
```
The address is a documentation example and must be replaced with an approved free address on the actual network. Creation and IP operations require the documented privileged execution context. Add the appropriate application dependency on this VIP and test failover; merely creating an IP resource does not automatically make an arbitrary application listen on it or restart correctly on another node.

CRSCTL add resource and VIP example

mnemonic.anchor: An application VIP gives clients a stable network endpoint for a Clusterware-managed application.

text:
Your four-node cluster runs Oracle 19c Clusterware and supports a mix of RAC databases from Oracle 10g Release 2 to Oracle 19c. All databases have one or more services defined. The Oracle 10g Release 2 database clients connect to the database instances using the public VIP. The Oracle 11g Release 2, 12c Release 1, and 19c clients connect to the database instances using the Single Client Access Name (SCAN). You must change the public VIPs.

Which three actions must be performed to change the VIPs on host01, the first node in the cluster? (Choose three.)

options.text: Use srvctl start vip to start the VIP on host01.
Use oifcfg setif to start the VIP on host01.
Use oifcfg setif to stop the VIP on host01.
Use srvctl modify nodeapps to change the VIP on host01.
Use srvctl stop vip to stop the VIP on host01.

explanation:
The key is A, D and E. The intended sequence is E, D, A: stop the old VIP, update its configured address, and start it with the new address. These are Clusterware resource operations, so SRVCTL is the relevant management interface.

E is correct because the documented VIP-address-change procedure stops the node VIP before changing its address. D is correct: `srvctl modify nodeapps -node host01 -address ...` updates the node-application VIP address configuration in the procedure described by Oracle. A is correct because the VIP then needs to be started. B and C are false because OIFCFG classifies and manages network interfaces; `oifcfg setif` is not a command to start or stop a VIP resource.

The client-generation details explain the impact of the change rather than selecting a different resource command. Older clients that name the node VIP may require connection-configuration updates. SCAN-aware clients continue using the stable SCAN name, assuming the SCAN network and service registration remain correct. SCAN is not itself the node VIP being changed.

The core resource operations look like:
```text
srvctl stop vip -node host01
srvctl modify nodeapps -node host01 -address 192.0.2.21/255.255.255.0/eth0
srvctl start vip -node host01
```
This example is not a full change procedure: stop or relocate affected services and listeners as documented, update DNS and hosts-file entries, and account for a subnet change separately. Run the address modification with the required privileged account. Validate the final configuration and listener service registration before releasing the maintenance window. The command's execution host does not have to be HOST01 simply because that is the target node; SRVCTL is cluster-aware.

text: Which two statements are true about server categorization in Oracle 19c Clusterware? (Choose two.)

options.text: Different nodes in a cluster may belong to separate administrator-defined categories.
All nodes in a cluster belong to the same Oracle-supplied category.
A server may be added to only one category using the crsctl utility.
All server attributes that may be used to determine the server category are discovered automatically by Oracle Clusterware.
All server attributes used for categorization are administrator modifiable.
Server categories can only be used for nodes running an application server.

explanation:
The key is A and B. Server categorization combines an Oracle-supplied base classification with optional administrator-defined categories that describe eligible hardware or deployment characteristics. Categories are expressions evaluated against server attributes; they are not a manually exclusive membership list.

A is correct because different nodes can match different administrator-defined categories. For example, a high-memory category can accept servers with sufficient memory, while another category uses an administrator-assigned location label. B is correct in the 19c supported architecture: Oracle documents the supplied `hub` category for standard and Flex clusters. Custom classifications supplement this supplied category rather than requiring every node to have the same custom classification.

C is false because a server can satisfy multiple category expressions. It is not limited to one administrator category through a one-time CRSCTL assignment. D is false: some useful attributes are discovered from the host, but others are explicitly administrator controlled. Examples are `SERVER_LABEL` and `CPU_EQUIVALENCY`, which Oracle documents with set/get commands. E is the opposite overstatement: not all server attributes are modifiable; role and physical/state information include read-only values. F incorrectly restricts this general placement facility to application servers; databases and other workloads can also use pools constrained by server category.

For a lab, inspect the server properties and an administrator label:
```text
crsctl status server host01 -p
crsctl get server label
```
A category expression can combine discovered CPU or memory values with a label representing a site or equipment class. Match the pool's `SERVER_CATEGORY` to the category rather than assuming the name itself moves the node. Some attribute changes require restarting the affected Clusterware stack before category evaluation uses their new values; plan such changes as configuration work, not as cosmetic relabeling.

Server labels, CPU equivalency and category commands

mnemonic.anchor: Categories are expressions evaluated against server attributes; they are not a manually exclusive membership list.

text:
Examine this command:

```text
SQL> ALTER TABLESPACE TBS1 ADD DATAFILE '+DATA(newtemplate)/ORCL/USERS/mytab.dbf' SIZE 100M;
```

Which two statements are required for this command to succeed? (Choose two.)

options.text: The DB_CREATE_FILE_DEST parameter must be set to +DATA(newtemplate).
newtemplate must be defined for the +DATA disk group.
Existing data files in TBS1 must also use the same template.
User-defined subdirectories ORCL and USERS must already exist.
The +DATA disk group should not be part of Flex ASM.

explanation:
The key is B and D. The filename uses the ASM alias-with-template form: the disk group is DATA, the selected template is newtemplate, and the desired alias is ORCL/USERS/mytab.dbf. A template controls file-creation characteristics, while an alias is a human-readable path to the underlying ASM file.

B is correct because the named template must exist in the disk group where the file is being created. A template in a different disk group does not satisfy the reference. D is correct because the intermediate alias directories must already exist; specifying a nested alias is not a request for Oracle to create an arbitrary directory hierarchy automatically.

A is false because the statement supplies a complete destination filename. `DB_CREATE_FILE_DEST` is useful for default Oracle Managed Files placement but is not mandatory for this explicitly named ASM file. C is false because templates are file-creation rules, not a requirement that all files of an existing tablespace use one identical template. E is false because Flex ASM does not prohibit alias names or user-defined templates.

Before issuing the database statement, a storage administrator can inspect the relevant objects:
```text
asmcmd lstmpl +DATA
asmcmd ls +DATA/ORCL/USERS/
```
Then the database administrator issues the ALTER TABLESPACE statement using the intended alias. A matching template and directory do not by themselves prove every other prerequisite: the disk group must be mounted and accessible, there must be sufficient usable capacity, the alias must be available, and the executing user must have the database privilege to add a file.

The subtle operational consequence is that a file created with a user-specified ASM alias is not an OMF file in the same sense as a purely system-managed filename. Do not assume that database object deletion will perform every desired alias/file cleanup; follow Oracle's documented file-management behavior.

sources.title: ASM alias-with-template names, directories and template requirements

mnemonic.anchor: The filename uses the ASM alias-with-template form: the disk group is DATA, the selected template is newtemplate, and the desired alias is ORCL/USERS/mytab.dbf.

text: Which two statements are true regarding the default service that is automatically created upon PDB creation in a RAC database environment? (Choose two.)

options.text: It is uniformly available on all instances for administrator-managed databases.
It cannot be used to automate the opening of the PDB by the Clusterware.
It is automatically registered in the OCR.
It is created and started on only one instance when using policy-managed database configuration.
It is not automatically registered in the OCR.

explanation:
The key is B and E. Creating a PDB creates a default database service bearing the PDB's name, but that automatic database service is not the same thing as an explicitly configured, Clusterware-managed application service.

B is correct: the automatic default PDB service cannot be used as the Clusterware service resource that drives the desired PDB open-state management. E is correct because creation of the PDB does not automatically register that default service as a managed service in the Oracle Cluster Registry. To obtain Clusterware placement, failover and lifecycle behavior, create an application service using SRVCTL with the PDB association.

A overstates availability: a PDB can be open on only selected CDB instances, and its default service is not a uniform Clusterware resource that forces it open everywhere. C is the opposite of E. D incorrectly gives the automatic default service singleton policy-managed placement semantics; cardinality is an attribute of the managed service you configure, not a universal property of the default PDB service.

For example, a policy-managed application service can be defined with a PDB association:
```text
srvctl add service -db CDB1 -service orders -pdb PDB_1 -serverpool prod_pool -cardinality singleton
srvctl start service -db CDB1 -service orders
```
The names are illustrative and the database/server-pool configuration must exist. Check both the service and the PDB open state after starting it. Use an application-specific service name for client connections so that workload placement and service goals can be controlled deliberately. Oracle treats default/internal services as management facilities; their existence is not a reason to bypass application-service configuration. The distinction to remember is database service creation versus OCR registration and Clusterware resource management.

Managing PDBs and services in RAC

text: Which three resources are managed using global concurrency control in an Oracle 19c RAC multi-instance database? (Choose three.)

options.text: Database block buffers
Mutexes
Redo log buffers
Latches
Enqueues
Cursors

explanation:
The intended key is A, E and F. RAC must preserve correctness when instances have separate memory structures but access one database. Some resources require cluster-wide coordination, while a latch or mutex used to protect an instance's own SGA remains a local synchronization mechanism.

A is correct: the Global Cache Service coordinates database block access and transfers between the buffer caches. If a second instance needs a block that another instance owns in an incompatible mode, the global protocol determines what must happen before access is granted. E is correct because global enqueues coordinate resources such as transaction and table locks across instances. F refers to global coordination of library-cache objects and their dependencies: DDL or an invalidation on one instance must not leave another instance using an incompatible definition.

B and D are false because mutexes and latches protect memory structures within an instance. The fact that a global request handler may use local latches internally does not make those latch objects globally owned synchronization resources. C is false because each instance owns its redo log buffer and LGWR writes its own redo thread; RAC does not create one globally shared redo buffer.

As a practical example, let session 1 update a row through instance 1 without committing. A session on instance 2 trying to update the same row must respect the transaction lock, while queries also require the correct block version. The buffer-coherence and transaction-lock mechanisms cooperate, but they solve different problems. Separately, altering a table can invalidate dependent SQL across instances; that illustrates the library-cache aspect represented by F.

Do not take F to mean cursor memory or execution state is physically shared between SGAs. Each instance has local structures. Global locks and invalidation protocols coordinate their use and consistency; Cache Fusion primarily concerns database block images, not shipping an instance's entire shared pool.

text: Which two actions guarantee that time is synchronized properly on all nodes in a cluster after installing Oracle Grid Infrastructure 19c? (Choose two.)

options.text: If network time protocol (NTP) time servers are unreachable on any cluster node, then Oracle Cluster Time Synchronization Service (CTSSD) will start automatically in active mode when the clusterware is started.
Configure network time protocol (NTP) on all cluster nodes, and then start the Oracle Cluster Time Synchronization Service (CTSSD) in active mode on all cluster nodes.

If network time protocol (NTP) is not configured properly on all cluster nodes, then Oracle Cluster Time Synchronization Service (CTSSD) will start automatically in active mode when the clusterware is started.
Configure network time protocol (NTP) on all cluster nodes; Oracle Cluster Time Synchronization Service (CTSSD) will then start automatically in observer mode when the clusterware is started.
Deactivate network time protocol (NTP) on all cluster nodes; Oracle Cluster Time Synchronization Service (CTSSD) will then start automatically in active mode when the clusterware is started.

explanation:
The key is D and E. CTSS chooses observer or active behavior according to whether it detects a vendor time-synchronization service. It is not a substitute that automatically takes control whenever the configured NTP server is temporarily unreachable.

D is correct for a properly configured and running NTP service across the cluster: CTSS observes time behavior while the vendor service performs synchronization. E is correct when the vendor service is stopped and deconfigured on all nodes: CTSS can run in active mode and synchronize cluster members using its reference-node mechanism.

A is false because remote NTP-server reachability is not the documented trigger for switching CTSS to active mode. An NTP daemon may still be present and running even when its upstream source is unreachable; in that case CTSS does not simply become a competing time authority. B is false because deliberately operating NTP and active CTSS simultaneously is not the supported design. C is false because the vague phrase “not configured properly” does not guarantee that CTSS will detect absence of the vendor service or that time will be correct.

Check the actual service mode rather than inferring it:
```text
crsctl check ctss
```
Then use the operating system's appropriate NTP/chrony inspection commands to verify synchronization to the approved time sources. Observer mode alone proves only that CTSS is not acting as the synchronizer; it does not prove the external time service is healthy.

There is also a version qualification: Oracle marks CTSS deprecated in 19c and recommends a supported vendor time service for new operational designs. The exam still tests CTSS's documented active/observer distinction. Ensure all nodes use the chosen method consistently, and do not equate internally synchronized cluster time with guaranteed accuracy against an external civil-time source.

CTSS active mode when no vendor service is detected

mnemonic.anchor: CTSS chooses observer or active behavior according to whether it detects a vendor time-synchronization service.

text:
Examine the output of the asmcmd and srvctl commands:

```text
$ asmcmd showclustermode
ASM cluster : Flex mode enabled

$ srvctl status asm -detail
ASM is running on host01, host03
ASM is enabled.

$ srvctl config asm
ASM home: /u01/app/12.1.0/grid
Password file: +DATA/orapwASM
ASM listener: LISTENER
ASM instance count: 2
Cluster ASM listener: ASMNET1LSNR_ASM

$ srvctl relocate asm -currentnode host03 -targetnode host02
```

Which three statements are true regarding the execution of this command based on the output shown? (Choose three.)

options.text: It fails because the ASM instance has not been shut down first on HOST03.
It succeeds and starts an ASM instance on HOST02 but the ASM instance on HOST03 is not shut down until all connected clients disconnect.
It succeeds and starts an ASM instance on HOST02 and shuts down the ASM instance on HOST03.
It succeeds and 19c database instances connected to the ASM instance on HOST03 can be reconnected to the ASM instance on HOST02.
It succeeds and 19c database instances connected to the ASM instance on HOST03 can be reconnected to the ASM instance on HOST01.
It fails because an ASM instance is not configured to run on HOST02.

explanation:
The intended corrected key is C, D and E, assuming the documented prerequisites for relocation are met. Relocation is an orchestrated move of the ASM resource: establish the destination instance, move eligible Flex ASM client connections, and stop the original ASM instance. It does not require a pre-existing, permanently pinned ASM instance on every candidate destination node.

C describes that completed relocation. D and E are possible because 19c Flex ASM clients can reconnect to available ASM instances, including the newly started instance on HOST02 or the remaining instance on HOST01. The client connection is for ASM metadata and management; with ordinary direct-storage Flex ASM clients, database block I/O still goes directly to shared disks.

A is false as a general explanation: an administrator does not first shut down the source ASM instance as a universal prerequisite to issuing a relocation operation. F misunderstands Flex ASM cardinality and placement: an instance count of two specifies the desired running count, not an immutable list of two allowed nodes. B is not a reliable completion description because it implies the source simply remains until clients choose to disconnect; eligible clients can be actively relocated/reconnected, after which the resource move completes.

Inspect the post-operation state:
```text
srvctl status asm -detail
srvctl config asm
```
From ASM, inspect `V$ASM_CLIENT` to determine actual client attachment. Do not predict a particular least-loaded instance solely from the node list.

This item has missing prerequisites. Oracle documents a bootstrap caveat where the node's Clusterware uses ASM, and the displayed Grid home is 12.1 rather than 19c. Without the resource dependencies and client mix, unconditional success is not established. CDE is the normal intended Flex ASM result, but the stem should explicitly assume relocation prerequisites are satisfied; it should not be treated as proof that this exact abbreviated environment always succeeds.

text:
You administer a six-instance, policy-managed, multitenant RAC database CDB1 with three PDBs: PDB_1,PDB_2, and PDB_3. Server pool prod_pool has a cardinality of three and all six hosts of the cluster are up.

Examine these commands executed on HOST01:

```text
$ srvctl add service -db CDB1 -pdb PDB_1 -service AR -serverpool prod_pool -cardinality singleton
$ srvctl start service -db CDB1 -service AR
```

Which two statements are true regarding the AR service? (Choose two.)

options.text: AR can fail over to any one of the available CDB1 instances.
AR runs as a singleton service in the server pool prod_pool and the AR service is available in each of the CDB1 instances.
AR can fail over to any other available CDB1 instance in prod_pool.
AR is available only on the CDB1 instance on HOST01.
AR is available on any one available CDB1 instance in prod_pool at any one time.

explanation:
The key is C and E. A policy-managed service is constrained by its configured server pool, and its cardinality determines how many eligible instances provide it. Executing the command on HOST01 does not itself select HOST01 as the permanent service host.

E is correct because `-cardinality singleton` makes AR available on one eligible CDB1 instance in prod_pool at a time. C is correct because a failure or planned relocation can move that service to another eligible instance inside the same pool. The pool has three servers, so it offers potential replacement capacity, not three simultaneous providers of this singleton service.

A is false because “any CDB1 instance” ignores the prod_pool boundary. Instances outside that server pool are not automatically eligible service destinations. B contradicts singleton cardinality by making the service available in each instance simultaneously; that would describe uniform placement within the pool. D wrongly treats the node running SRVCTL as the placement directive. The command contains no such fixed HOST01 placement instruction.

For a practical check:
```text
srvctl config service -db CDB1 -service AR
srvctl status service -db CDB1 -service AR
srvctl status database -db CDB1
```
Compare service configuration with actual instance and server-pool membership. Check the PDB association too: an application connecting through AR reaches PDB_1, not any arbitrary PDB in the CDB. Service management can arrange the required PDB availability on the selected instance according to the supported RAC PDB-service workflow.

The six-instance wording should not distract from the relevant placement domain. Whether the database has other instances elsewhere does not enlarge this service's configured server pool. Also, “can fail over” means another suitable running or startable provider is available; it is not a promise of successful failover when all pool servers or required dependencies have failed.

text: Which three statements are true concerning activation of a user-defined policy in Oracle 19c Clusterware? (Choose three.)

options.text: When a policy is activated, resources can be automatically stopped to comply with the policy definition.
An administrator-defined policy may be activated using the srvctl utility.
When a policy is first created, it is initially inactive.
When a policy is first created, it is initially active.
When a policy is activated, resources cannot be automatically started to comply with the policy definition.
When a policy is activated, nodes may be reassigned to server pools based on the policy definition.

explanation:
The key is A, C and F. Creating a policy stores a potential cluster configuration. Activating it asks Clusterware to make the running allocation conform to that definition, which can involve moving servers and changing where resources run.

C is correct because `crsctl add policy` does not activate the newly added policy. D is therefore false. F is correct: different pool minima, maxima, importance and eligibility requirements can cause nodes to be reassigned between server pools. A is correct because an instance or application resource may need to stop on a server that is leaving its current pool or becoming ineligible for its placement.

B names the wrong policy-control interface. Clusterware configuration policies are administered through the CRSCTL policy/policyset facility, not by an SRVCTL activate-policy command. SRVCTL does manage database and service resources, but that does not make it the command interface for every cluster policy operation. E is false because policy enforcement can start resources as well as stop them. The example in Oracle's policy guide shows resources following the server allocation established by the newly active policy.

An illustrative policy lifecycle is:
```text
crsctl add policy NightTime -attr "DESCRIPTION=nighttime"
crsctl status policyset
crsctl modify policyset -attr "LAST_ACTIVATED_POLICY=NightTime"
```
Define the intended server-pool settings before activation; merely adding a policy name is not a complete capacity plan. Inspect resource and pool status afterward and compare with the intended workload requirements.

Treat activation as an operational change. A syntactically valid policy can still stop important work if its constraints reassign a node or reduce capacity. Keep a recoverable policy-set export, understand the resource dependencies, and evaluate the effects before applying it to a production cluster. The important distinction is inactive configuration storage versus active enforcement against real servers and workloads.
