text: Which two methods exist for enabling the collection of additional resource debugging information for specific resources controlled by Oracle 19c Clusterware? (Choose two.)

options.text: Use the crsctl set trace res "resource_name=debugging_level" command.
Use the crsctl set log res "resource_name=debugging_level" command.
Set the environment variable _USR_ORA_DEBUG=1 and then stop and restart the resource that requires resource debugging data to be collected.
Use the cluvfy comp command for the specific resource within a component.

explanation:
A and B are the bank's intended pair: change trace or log verbosity for a named Clusterware resource rather than treating CVU validation as a resource-debugging switch. The unambiguous documented resource recipe in the 19c CRSCTL reference is `crsctl set log res "resource_name=debugging_level"`.

B is correct in that form. The level is a supported numeric verbosity value, not the literal text “debugging_level2”; the option uses a placeholder for the desired value. A follows the parallel trace-control idea, but the current 19c reference is less explicit: it documents both `set log` and `set trace` for modules/components, then gives the resource-specific syntax under `set log res`. Therefore the exact `set trace res` spelling in A should be confirmed with the installed CRSCTL help or Oracle Support for the deployed RU, rather than silently labelling it as independently proven by that resource-specific paragraph.

C is false because setting an arbitrary environment variable in an administrator's shell does not generally reconfigure a running Clusterware agent's resource debugging. Agent environments and supported debugging configuration are explicit; `_USR_ORA_DEBUG=1` is not the documented general method here. D is false because CVU verifies configuration and prerequisites. It does not enable persistent verbose tracing for a named application resource.

For example, the documented log workflow includes:
```text
crsctl status resource
crsctl set log res "my_application=5"
```
Run the debugging change with the documented privileges and choose the exact resource name. Capture the incident evidence, then restore the normal verbosity using the syntax appropriate to the installed release. High verbosity can produce substantial trace volume. Retain AB as the intended key, but keep this item's exact trace syntax flagged until confirmed for the target 19c installation.

sources.title: CRSCTL dynamic debugging, module trace and resource-specific log syntax

review_note: B resource-log syntax is explicitly documented; A exact set trace res syntax is not unambiguously covered by the current resource-specific 19c documentation. AB retained as intended pair pending installed-help/support confirmation.

mnemonic.anchor: The unambiguous documented resource recipe in the 19c CRSCTL reference is `crsctl set log res "resource_name=debugging_level"`.

text: Which three statements are true about diagnostic reporting for the OCR and OLR files? (Choose three.)

options.text: The OCRCHECK utility can check the OLR in an online fashion with the clusterware running on all nodes.
The OCRCONFIG utility can be used to repair a corrupt OCR file in an online fashion with the clusterware running on all nodes.
The CLUVFY utility can check the integrity of the OCR but not the OLR.
The OCRDUMP utility can dump specific keys from the OLR in an online fashion with the clusterware running on all nodes.
The OCRDUMP utility can dump specific keys from the OCR in an online fashion with the clusterware running on all nodes.

explanation:
C, D and E are the defensible answers when integrity means checking registry contents, with a qualification for C. The original A/D/E key overlooked the supported offline procedure for OCRCHECK.

Option A is false as a supported operational procedure: Oracle supports ocrcheck -local when both CRS and OHAS stacks are offline on the local node. A command might execute online without its result being a supported reliable contents-integrity assessment.

Option B confuses registry configuration repair with restoring corrupt contents. OCRCONFIG -repair reconciles local OCR configuration after changes made while a node was unavailable; it is not a universal online repair of corrupt OCR data.

Option C is true in the narrow contents-integrity sense: CVU has cluvfy comp olr, but Oracle explicitly says this does not verify the integrity of OLR contents; use OCRCHECK for that. Therefore claiming that CVU has no OLR check at all would also be incorrect.

Option D is true: OCRDUMP -local can display selected OLR keys. Option E is true for selected OCR keys. Dumping readable contents and checking all blocks for corruption are different diagnostic tasks.

Practical approach: identify whether you need a configuration display, a selected-key dump, a contents-integrity check, or restoration. Choose the utility and stack state accordingly, use the required administrative privileges, and maintain registry backups. Do not infer that every OCR utility requires the same online/offline state.

sources.title: Oracle Database 19c — CVU OLR verification scope

review_note: C is defensible only for OLR CONTENTS integrity; CVU does provide an OLR configuration/check command. A is unsupported online under current 19c OCRCHECK notes.

mnemonic.anchor: C, D and E are the defensible answers when integrity means checking registry contents, with a qualification for C.

text: Which two statements are true about resources defined by an administrator and registered with Oracle 19c Clusterware for high availability? (Choose two.)

options.text: An administrator-managed resource can be started manually using srvctl.
A policy-managed resource can be started manually using crsctl.
An administrator-managed resource can be started manually using crsctl.
The action script is automatically set when using a policy-managed resource.
A policy-managed resource can be started manually using srvctl.
Resource dependencies are automatically set when using a policy-managed resource.

explanation:
Options B and C are correct for administrator-defined application resources. The important distinction is resource ownership, rather than whether placement is administrator managed or policy managed. CRSCTL manages generic third-party application resources; SRVCTL manages the Oracle-defined object types it understands.

Option A is false for the generic resource described here. Calling a resource administrator managed does not register it as a database, listener or other SRVCTL object. Option B is true: CRSCTL can request a policy-managed application resource to start, with Clusterware evaluating its placement rules. Option C is true for an administrator-managed application resource as well.

Option D is false. The action implementation comes from the resource type, agent and configured attributes; a placement policy does not invent application-specific start/stop/check behavior. Option E repeats A's utility mismatch. Option F is false: the administrator must express dependencies on file systems, networks or other application resources. Placement policy cannot infer them automatically.

For a previously registered application:

```text
crsctl status resource my_app -p
crsctl start resource my_app
crsctl status resource my_app -t
```

Inspect its type and dependency attributes before starting it. For Oracle resources named with the ora. prefix, use SRVCTL unless Oracle Support explicitly directs otherwise. This resource-ownership rule prevents applying the generic-resource answer indiscriminately to Oracle database resources.

mnemonic.anchor: for administrator-defined application resources.

text: Which two benefits are obtained by using Affinity to reduce global resource contention? (Choose two.)

options.text: Oracle RAC affinity for partitioned tables routes all database requests for a partition tables to a single Oracle RAC instance leading to higher Oracle RAC performance and scalability because of improved cache locality and reduced internode synchronization and block pings of the partition tables.

Oracle RAC affinity for partitioned tables routes database requests to Oracle RAC instances in such a way that each instance always gets requests for a disjoint subset of rows in the database, this affinity leads to higher Oracle RAC performance and scalability because of improved cache locality and reduced internode synchronization and block pings.

Oracle RAC affinity for partitioned tables routes database requests to all available Oracle RAC instances evenly to create a global affinity in such a way that each instance always gets an even number of requests leading to higher Oracle RAC performance by using a higher levels of available global cache to reduce global resource contention.

To enhance the performance of distributed transactions with applications server that provides XA affinity, you can automatically spawn new dedicated database RAC instances to isolate distributed transaction.

To enhance the performance of distributed transactions with applications server that provides XA affinity, you can direct all branches of a distributed transaction to a single instance in the cluster to improve cache locality and reduce internode synchronization and block pings.

explanation:
Options B and E are best supported. Affinity keeps related work near the instance that owns or caches the relevant data, reducing cross-instance transfers and synchronization rather than merely equalizing connection counts.

Option A overstates the routing granularity. Affinity for partitioned tables does not route every request for an entire table to one instance: different keys and partitions can have different instance affinities. Option B closely matches Oracle's RAC Sharding description: key-based routing creates affinity between disjoint row subsets and instances. Requests must supply the routing key to obtain that benefit; keyless requests can still follow normal load balancing.

Option C describes even distribution, not data affinity. Equal connection counts can still increase contention when every session modifies the same hot data. Option D is false: XA affinity does not automatically create dedicated RAC instances. Option E is true: routing the branches of one distributed transaction to one instance reduces coordination overhead, provided the connection pool or application server preserves XA affinity.

Imagine a table partitioned by customer region. Requests for different regions can use their routing keys to reach different instances. Separately, two XA branches updating one order should retain transaction affinity while unrelated transactions are balanced elsewhere. These are distinct scopes: data ownership and transaction identity. Neither replaces locking, recovery or application design to avoid hot records.

sources.title: Oracle Database 19c — RAC Sharding and XA affinity

mnemonic.anchor: Options B and E are best supported.

text: Which method should be used to convert a single-instance Oracle 19c Database to a RAC Database?

options.text: Using the rconfig utility to migrate the database to shared storage and then using DBCA to start one or more RAC database instances on the cluster
Using DBCA to migrate the database to shared storage and then to start one or more RAC database instances on the cluster
Using the rconfig utility to create a template from the single-instance database and then using DBCA to create a RAC database on the cluster using that template
Using DBCA to create a template from the single-instance database and then to create a RAC database on the cluster using that template

explanation:
Option D describes the complete DBCA template workflow offered by these choices. A template containing structure and data supplies the source image; DBCA then creates a RAC database using the image, shared storage and cluster-specific configuration.

Option A combines tools misleadingly. RCONFIG is itself a supported conversion tool under its prerequisites; it does more than move files and leave DBCA to finish simply by starting instances. Option B also reduces conversion to file movement and startup. RAC needs cluster-enabled control-file attributes, redo threads, undo, parameters, networking and Clusterware registration. Storage movement alone is insufficient.

Option C assigns template creation to the wrong utility. DBCA generates the preconfigured database image/template. Option D correctly uses DBCA for both image creation and RAC deployment. Oracle also documents RCONFIG, so D must not be interpreted as the only supported conversion method in the product.

In practice, create a template including structure and data, validate the destination cluster, make the image available on a cluster node, then select it while provisioning RAC. Confirm shared-storage access from every selected node and a RAC-enabled home on those nodes. DBCA configures the RAC-specific components and registers the database. Validate application services and recovery before retiring the source. Starting an additional instance alone does not convert an arbitrary single-instance database into RAC.

mnemonic.anchor: Option D describes the complete DBCA template workflow offered by these choices.

text:
Examine this command:

```text
SQL> CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE pdb3 FROM pdb1;
```

Which three conditions must be true for successful execution of this command on a RAC database? (Choose three.)

options.text: The source PDB must be closed on the CDB instance from where the command is executed.
The source PDB must be in READ ONLY mode on all CDB instances if the CDB is in No Archive mode.
The source PDB must use a global temporary tablespace.
It can be executed only by a common user with the CREATE PLUGGABLE DATABASE system privilege connected to the root container.
Oracle Managed Files must be enabled or PDB_FILE_NAME_CONVERT must be set.
All running CDB instances must be open in restricted mode.

explanation:
Options B, D and E are correct for this exact statement. It clones a local PDB and supplies neither FILE_NAME_CONVERT nor CREATE_FILE_DEST, so source state and an implicit destination naming mechanism matter.

Option A is false: the source must not be closed on the instance executing the clone. In NOARCHIVELOG mode, the source must be protected against changes; Option B correctly requires read-only mode on RAC instances where it is open. With ARCHIVELOG and local undo,19c can instead hot-clone a read/write source.

Option C is false: a global temporary tablespace is not the clone prerequisite. Option D identifies the normal CDB-root context and common user with the required privilege. The account also needs the source-PDB privileges specified by the cloning procedure; a grant in the wrong container is insufficient.

Option E is correct because this statement omits explicit destination naming: OMF can generate names or PDB_FILE_NAME_CONVERT can map source names to distinct clone names. Option F is false: every CDB instance need not be restricted.

After cloning:

```sql
SELECT name, open_mode FROM v$pdbs;
ALTER PLUGGABLE DATABASE pdb3 OPEN;
```

The new PDB's initial mounted state is separate from the required source open state. Check file-name separation before opening the clone, then validate its service and application access.

sources.title: Oracle Database 19c — Local PDB clone prerequisites

mnemonic.anchor: It clones a local PDB and supplies neither FILE_NAME_CONVERT nor CREATE_FILE_DEST, so source state and an implicit destination naming mechanism matter.

text:
Examine this command and output:

```text
[root@host01 ~]# /sbin/acfsutil snap create snap001 /u01/app/grid/acfsmount/
acfsutil snap create: Snapshot operation is complete.

[root@host01 ~]# /sbin/acfsutil snap create -p snap001 snap002 /u01/app/grid/acfsmount/
```

Which statement must be true for the successful execution of the second command?

options.text: The disk group compatibility attribute for ADVM must be set to 12.1 or higher.
The parent snapshot must be read-only.
The underlying ADVM volume must be configured with high redundancy.
The parent snapshot must be read/write.

explanation:
Option A is correct. Creating a snapshot from an existing ACFS snapshot requires COMPATIBLE.ADVM of at least 12.1. The -p snap001 argument identifies a parent snapshot; it does not impose the read-only-parent requirement asserted in the original explanation.

Option B is not a general prerequisite. The first command happens to create a read-only snapshot because that is the default without -r or -w. An observed default is different from a rule that every parent must be read-only. Option C is false: high redundancy is not required for snapshot creation; ASM mirroring and ACFS point-in-time views solve different problems. Option D is false for the same reason as B: the parent need not be read/write.

The second command also defaults to a read-only child. It would need -w to request a read-write child; the previous explanation described this incorrectly.

Inspect relationships and types with:

```text
acfsutil snap info -t /u01/app/grid/acfsmount/
```

Before testing parent-based creation, check compatibility and the restrictions concerning older 11.2 snapshots and incomplete deletion cleanup. An operation can fail even after meeting the compatibility minimum. A snapshot is space-efficient storage within the same file system, not an independent off-site backup. Creating a child snapshot does not protect against losing the entire underlying disk group or volume.

sources.title: Oracle Database 19c — Snapshot syntax and restrictions

mnemonic.anchor: Creating a snapshot from an existing ACFS snapshot requires COMPATIBLE.ADVM of at least 12.1.

text: Which three statements are true about the Oracle Clusterware 19c Flex Cluster architecture? (Choose three.)

options.text: Each hub node must be connected to storage shared across all hub nodes.
Each leaf node must be connected to storage shared across all cluster nodes.
Each leaf node must be connected to storage shared across all leaf nodes.
Leaf nodes require direct access to the voting disks.
Hub nodes require direct access to the OCR file.
Hub nodes require direct access to the voting disks.

explanation:
A, E and F are the intended answers for the historical hub-and-leaf architecture. However, the 19c framing is obsolete: Oracle desupported Leaf Nodes in Grid Infrastructure 19c, where all Flex Cluster nodes function as Hub Nodes.

Option A describes storage-connected Hub Nodes. Options E and F identify shared OCR and voting access associated with that tier. Hubs anchor the cluster and participate directly in its shared-storage configuration.

Options B and C wrongly require shared-storage access for Leaf Nodes. The historical leaf tier did not require direct shared-storage connectivity. Option D consequently imposes a direct-voting-disk requirement absent from the old leaf model. The leaf depended on its hub connection instead of behaving as another storage-connected hub.

An older architecture diagram may show a compute-oriented leaf connected to a storage-connected hub. It helps explain the original design, but does not justify adding a 19c leaf node to a supported production cluster. Before upgrading, inventory roles and check 19c release changes rather than assuming an earlier training diagram still defines an available deployment.

The study distinction is therefore twofold: A/E/F captures the old bank's intended storage responsibilities, while the release note explains why the leaf distractors are historical. Do not mistake their false requirements for evidence that leaf deployment remains supported in 19c. Flex ASM and Flex Cluster are also different concepts; remote ASM metadata access does not restore the desupported leaf architecture.

sources.title: Oracle Database 19c — Historical Flex Cluster design

review_note: Leaf Nodes are desupported in GI 19c; intended AEF retained as historical architecture with an explicit release caveat.

mnemonic.anchor: A, E and F are the intended answers for the historical hub-and-leaf architecture.

text: Which four statements are true concerning the upgrading of Oracle Grid Infrastructure 19c? (Choose four.)

options.text: The cluster verification utility cluvfy.sh can verify that the cluster is ready for an upgrade.
The cluster verification utility cluvfy.sh can generate fixup scripts to run on all nodes of the cluster.
The ORACLE_SID environment variable must be set to the SID of the ASM instance in the installation owner's environment.
The ORACLE_HOME environment variable must be set to the Grid Infrastructure home directory in the installation owner's environment.
The upgrade must be done in-place.
Upgrade validation may be done using the Oracle Universal Installer which in turn invokes the built-in cluster verification utility.
The upgrade must be done out-of-place.

explanation:
Options A, B, F and G are correct. Grid Infrastructure release-upgrade preparation combines readiness checks, supported OS fixups and installation into a separate Grid home.

Option A is true: CVU validates cluster upgrade readiness. Option B is true for checks supporting fixups: CVU can generate scripts to correct supported prerequisite failures on affected nodes. It cannot repair every hardware or application issue automatically.

Options C and D are false: the installation owner's ORACLE_SID and ORACLE_HOME should be unset as directed by the upgrade checklist, not pointed to the old ASM instance/home. Option E is false because a release upgrade does not replace the old home's binaries in place. Option F is true: OUI integrates CVU checks, so a separate CVU invocation is useful preparation but not the sole way validation occurs. Option G is true: the upgrade uses a new Grid home.

For example, stage the target release in a separate directory, run pre-upgrade checks, resolve failures, then execute the upgrade workflow and its prompted privileged configuration scripts. Keep the existing home and recovery information for the documented rollback path. Merely creating the new directory does not complete the upgrade: configuration changes the active cluster version and participating nodes must reach the required state.

Distinguish this release-upgrade requirement from procedures for applying an individual patch/RU. Upgrade, patching and switching homes describe related but different maintenance operations.

mnemonic.anchor: Grid Infrastructure release-upgrade preparation combines readiness checks, supported OS fixups and installation into a separate Grid home.

text: Which two statements are true regarding ASM when installing Oracle Grid Infrastructure 19c? (Choose two.)

options.text: If ASM disk groups are configured for the Clusterware files, then ASM must be used for all databases on the cluster.
The Installer permits the creation of a disk group to be used for the Recovery Area for the ASM instance.
If no ASM disk groups are specified during installation, then ASM instances are not started after the installation completes on any cluster node.
ASM disk groups used for voting files and OCR files require a quorum failgroup.
The Installer permits the creation of a disk group for use by the voting disks and OCR file.

explanation:
E is unambiguously true. D is the intended second choice, but the phrase require a quorum failgroup needs qualification: the documented voting-quorum design is not a universal requirement to explicitly create a QUORUM-only failure group for every OCR/voting configuration.

Option A is false: using ASM for Clusterware storage does not force every database to use ASM for all its files. Option B is false because an ASM instance is not an ordinary database requiring its own FRA. Option C cannot be inferred merely from omitting a database-data disk group; Clusterware storage and the actual ASM configuration still matter.

Option D reflects the quorum availability design discussed in installation guides. It must not be read as permitting OCR in a QUORUM-only failure group: the SQL reference excludes OCR, database files and dynamic volumes from those groups, although voting files can be placed there. REGULAR failure groups and external-redundancy configurations make the unqualified requirement problematic. Option E correctly describes installer-created storage for OCR/voting files.

In practice, design the disk group according to supported redundancy and real failure domains, rather than adding a QUORUM-marked disk because an exam explanation says so. Verify the resulting storage and voting layout. D/E is retained as the intended key, with this ambiguity stated so that it does not become an unsafe universal storage rule.
review_note: D overstates a universal requirement: dedicated QUORUM-only failure groups cannot hold OCR and are not required for every configuration. Intended DE retained with caveat.

mnemonic.anchor: Option C cannot be inferred merely from omitting a database-data disk group; Clusterware storage and the actual ASM configuration still matter.

text:
A cluster running 19c Grid Infrastructure supports both Oracle 11g to 19c RAC databases using ASM. The COMPATIBLE.ASM, COMPATIBLE.RDBMS, and COMPATIBLE.ADVM parameters are currently set to 11.2 for all diskgroups. You must support these capabilities in all diskgroups:

1. ACFS Replication
2. ACFS Encryption

To what minimum values must the compatible attributes be set?

options.text: Set COMPATIBLE.ASM to 11.2, COMPATIBLE.RDBMS to 12.1, and COMPATIBLE.ADVM to 11.2.
Set COMPATIBLE.ASM to 12.1, COMPATIBLE.RDBMS to 12.1, and COMPATIBLE.ADVM to 12.1.
Set COMPATIBLE.ASM to 11.2, COMPATIBLE.RDBMS to 12.1, and COMPATIBLE.ADVM to 12.1.
Set COMPATIBLE.ASM to 12.1, COMPATIBLE.RDBMS to 11.2, and COMPATIBLE.ADVM to 12.1.
Set COMPATIBLE.ASM to 11.2, COMPATIBLE.RDBMS to 11.2, and COMPATIBLE.ADVM to 11.2.

explanation:
D is the intended legacy answer, but no option specifies the minimum for the snapshot-based ACFS replication documented in 19c. That procedure requires both COMPATIBLE.ASM and COMPATIBLE.ADVM at least 12.2. D must therefore be treated as historical, not a verified current numeric minimum.

Option A incorrectly advances only the database-client compatibility. Option B unnecessarily raises COMPATIBLE.RDBMS to 12.1, conflicting with continued access by older clients. Option C leaves ASM below the required ADVM feature level. Option D illustrates the correct principle: advance ASM/ADVM feature levels while keeping RDBMS compatibility appropriate for the oldest database client. Its 12.1 value is nevertheless insufficient for documented snapshot-based replication. Option E leaves both feature levels too low.

Older log-based replication descriptions explain why such bank versions exist. Protocol1 was deprecated in19.3 after snapshot-based version2 appeared in 12.2. Encryption has separate minima/platform qualifications, so evaluate the capabilities independently.

Before changing compatibility, inventory clients and ACFS features:

```sql
SELECT name, value FROM v$asm_attribute
WHERE name LIKE 'compatible.%';
```

Raising compatibility may be irreversible. In a real 19c configuration, determine the supported replication generation first; do not blindly apply D's numbers. The key remains visible to explain the legacy intent, while this warning prevents representing 12.1 as the current snapshot-replication minimum.

sources.title: Oracle Database 19c — Replication generation and compatibility

review_note: No option gives ASM/ADVM 12.2, the documented snapshot-replication minimum. Intended legacy D retained as ambiguous.

mnemonic.anchor: D is the intended legacy answer, but no option specifies the minimum for the snapshot-based ACFS replication documented in 19c.

text: Which three statements are true about the services created when the DBCA is used to create a RAC database? (Choose three.)

options.text: A server pool must be created with SRVCTL before creating a policy-managed RAC database that uses that server pool for a service.
They can be policy managed for a multitenant database.
Policy-managed services specified for a database allow the creation of a new server pool using DBCA.
They can be administrator managed for a multitenant database.
Singleton services are not permitted for multitenant databases.

explanation:
B, C and D are the intended conceptual answers, with a tooling caveat: Oracle 19c says cluster-managed application services are no longer managed through DBCA; use SRVCTL or Enterprise Manager. DBCA still creates the default database service and can create/select server pools during database creation.

Option A is false: the pool need not always have been created beforehand using SRVCTL. DBCA can offer a new pool when the active configuration and available servers permit it. Option B is true as a deployment capability: multitenant databases can use policy-managed services. Option C captures DBCA's pool-creation capability, but attributing it to defining application services is imprecise in the modern workflow. Option D is also true as a capability: CDB/PDB workloads can use administrator-managed services. Option E is false: multitenant does not prohibit singleton services.

For example, create a CDB using the desired database management model, then create an application service with SRVCTL, specifying its PDB and preferred/available instances or server pool. Verify its configuration and connect the application to that service. Avoid treating the default database service as a substitute for a managed production application service.

BCD is retained because it reflects these service/pool capabilities, but the stem should not teach that DBCA 19c is the general interface for creating and administering all cluster-managed application services.

sources.title: Oracle Database 19c — DBCA server pools and default service

review_note: BCD is intended capability answer; stem conflates DBCA pool/database creation with application-service management, no longer handled by DBCA 19c.

mnemonic.anchor: DBCA still creates the default database service and can create/select server pools during database creation.

text: Which three statements are true about accessing ASM files? (Choose three.)

options.text: Database instances perform read I/O using an ASM instance as an I/O Server.
Database instances can write metadata to ASM diskgroups.
Database instances perform read I/O directly to ASM Disks.
ASM instances can write metadata to ASM diskgroups.
If a database instance writes to an ASM-based datafile whose redundancy attribute is set to mirror, then the ASM instance writes the mirror copy.

explanation:
C and D are unambiguous. B supplies a third answer only if metadata includes database metadata stored inside database files, such as file/segment headers. If metadata means ASM allocation/disk-group metadata exclusively, B is false and the choose-three instruction has only two correct statements.

Option A is false for conventional direct-storage ASM: database block reads do not pass through the ASM instance acting as an I/O server. Databases obtain layout information from ASM, then access disks directly. IOServer deployments are a distinct named architecture, not a justification for treating an ordinary ASM instance as the data path.

Option B is true in the broad database-file sense. Database processes write their own metadata blocks in files stored in ASM. This does not make them managers of ASM allocation metadata. Option C correctly describes direct database reads. Option D is true because ASM maintains its own disk-group/file-allocation metadata.

Option E is false. ASM allocates primary/mirror extents and supplies their layout; database I/O writes the mirrored copies. It is wrong to say DBWn writes one copy and the ASM instance writes the other.

For diagnosis, distinguish the control path—allocation and extent maps—from the data path—block reads/writes. ASM CPU utilization is not a count of all database blocks passing through it. B/C/D uses the broad metadata meaning while preserving the wording warning.

sources.title: Oracle Database 19c — ASM metadata and direct I/O
Oracle Database 19c — Flex ASM data/control paths

review_note: B true for database/file metadata, false if restricted to ASM allocation metadata. BCD uses broad wording; distinction explicit.

mnemonic.anchor: B supplies a third answer only if metadata includes database metadata stored inside database files, such as file/segment headers.

text: Which statement describes the usage of Dynamic Service Fallback in Oracle RAC 19c?

options.text: Dynamic Service Fallback allows a service to relocate to an available instance when the service is stopped on a preferred instance.

Dynamic Service Fallback allows a service to fall back to a preferred instance when the available instance performance falls below a specified threshold after it was failed over to an available instance.

To enable Dynamic Service Fallback, you should specify the level of performance of a preferred instance for a service to be relocated to an available instance by setting the -failback attribute of a service to "Low, Medium, or High".
Dynamic Service Fallback allows a service to fall back to a preferred instance when it becomes available after it was failed over to an available instance.

explanation:
Option D is correct. When the service -failback attribute is YES, a service that failed over to an available instance after exhausting preferred instances can automatically return when a preferred instance becomes available.

Option A describes movement away from a preferred instance, not failback. Stopping a service manually also differs from losing an instance: administrative intent and command options affect later placement. Option B invents a performance-threshold trigger; the documented trigger is preferred-instance availability. Option C invents Low/Medium/High values: the attribute uses YES/NO. Option D describes the behavior introduced in19.3.

For an existing service:

```text
srvctl modify service -db crm -service orders -failback YES
srvctl config service -db crm -service orders
```

Use the actual registered names. This changes placement of a service resource; it does not move a server process's memory or an in-flight transaction between instances. Draining, FAN and application-continuity configuration affect the client experience.

Avoiding unnecessary movement is normally intentional: a service already running on an available instance has its desired cardinality, and moving again can disturb clients. Enable failback when restoring the preferred topology is worth that extra movement. Test recovery as well as initial failure: a successful failover alone does not prove the service will return to the preferred instance.

mnemonic.anchor: Option A describes movement away from a preferred instance, not failback.

text:
Examine these descriptions of ASM instance shutdown behavior:

1. The ASM instance shuts down immediately without an orderly dismount of disk groups.
2. Active SQL statements are allowed to complete before an orderly dismount of all disk groups occurs and then the ASM instance shuts down without waiting for connected sessions to disconnect. If any ASM clients are connected to the instance, then the shutdown returns an error.
3. Active SQL statements are allowed to complete before an orderly dismount of all of disk groups occurs and then the ASM instance shuts down after waiting for connected sessions to disconnect. If any ASM clients are connected to the instance, then the shutdown returns an error.

Which two lists are correct matches for these descriptions? (Choose two.)

options.text: 2 = NORMAL, 3 = TRANSACTIONAL, 1 = ABORT
2 = NORMAL, 3 = IMMEDIATE, 1 = ABORT
3 = NORMAL, 2 = TRANSACTIONAL, 1 = ABORT
3 = NORMAL, 2 = ABORT, 1 = IMMEDIATE
3 = NORMAL, 2 = IMMEDIATE, 1 = ABORT

explanation:
Options C and E give the correct mappings. Description1 is ABORT; description2 is either IMMEDIATE or TRANSACTIONAL; description3 is NORMAL. The equivalence of the middle two modes is specific to ASM, whose instance does not host ordinary database transactions.

Option A reverses NORMAL and TRANSACTIONAL. Option B incorrectly assigns NORMAL to description2. Option C is correct: NORMAL waits for connected sessions, while TRANSACTIONAL behaves like IMMEDIATE. Option D calls orderly description2 ABORT and abrupt description1 IMMEDIATE, reversing their meaning. Option E correctly names description2 IMMEDIATE.

Do not transfer SHUTDOWN TRANSACTIONAL behavior from an ordinary RDBMS to ASM. For ASM, consider active ASM SQL, user sessions, dependent database clients and disk-group dismounts, not application transactions in ASM tables.

Before maintenance, inspect clients and ADVM/ACFS consumers. Under the documented conventional dependencies, NORMAL/IMMEDIATE/TRANSACTIONAL return an error if database instances remain connected. ABORT bypasses orderly dismount and can stop dependent databases. Flex ASM availability can affect how dependencies are serviced; follow that deployment's procedure.

The exam mapping is:

```text
1 -> ABORT
2 -> IMMEDIATE or TRANSACTIONAL
3 -> NORMAL
```

A successful ASM shutdown is not proof that file systems were safely prepared. Dismount ACFS consumers according to the maintenance procedure before stopping their underlying storage; otherwise application I/O errors or unwritten metadata can result.

text: Which two statements are true about Oracle Clustered ASM performance? (Choose two.)

options.text: Data files, redo logs, and RMAN backup pieces must be stored in different ASM disk groups for optimal performance.
All ASM Disks belonging to a disk group should be of the same size for optimal performance.
Hardware-based mirroring combined with ASM mirroring guarantees optimal performance.
All ASM Disks belonging to a disk group should have the same hardware specifications and storage attributes for optimal performance.
To improve performance a database must have two disk groups; one for data and one for the fast recovery area.

explanation:
Options B and D are correct design recommendations. ASM distributes file extents across disks, so devices with comparable capacity, latency and throughput avoid a subset of storage dominating response time.

Option A is false because must is too strong: datafiles, redo logs and backup pieces do not universally need three different groups for optimum performance. Storage characteristics, redundancy and failure isolation guide grouping. Option B is correct as a steady-state sizing recommendation. Different capacities may be supported, but uniform devices simplify balanced capacity and I/O behavior.

Option C offers an impossible guarantee. Combining hardware and ASM mirroring can add write work and capacity cost; it never guarantees optimum performance for every workload. Option D correctly recommends similar device characteristics: matching nominal capacity does not make a slow and a fast disk equivalent. Option E turns another recommendation into a universal requirement. Separating DATA and FRA is useful for recovery/failure isolation, but precisely two groups is not a universal performance prerequisite.

For example, seven fast devices plus one slow device can give uneven latency despite distributed extents. Compare individual-device response times before increasing database memory or blaming RAC interconnect traffic. During a migration, old/new devices can temporarily coexist while ASM rebalances. That supported temporary configuration does not invalidate the steady-state recommendation. Size for capacity and I/O service characteristics, and check whether multiple advertised LUNs actually share the same underlying physical bottleneck.

mnemonic.anchor: ASM distributes file extents across disks, so devices with comparable capacity, latency and throughput avoid a subset of storage dominating response time.

text: Which two statements are true about ASM Cloud File System (ACFS) replication? (Choose two.)

options.text: Replication is automatically terminated if the primary file system has less than 2 GB free space.
ACFS auditing information is replicated from the primary file system to the standby file system.
Standby redo log files are required on the standby site for synchronous redo transport.
The privilege SYSREPL has been introduced for ACFS replication.
One site of an ACFS replication configuration can host both primary and standby file systems.

explanation:
B and E are verified for the ACFS replication model documented in 19c. The original D selection is wrong: SYSREPL is not an ACFS administrative privilege. The choose-three question mixes old log-based replication wording with the modern snapshot-based model.

Option A derives from legacy protocol 1 descriptions: ACFS attempts to terminate replication below 2GB primary free space. It is not a guarantee or the documented rule for the snapshot-based procedure; protocol 1 was deprecated in19.3. Never use that fixed threshold as your capacity-management strategy.

Option B is true: primary audit policies and trails can be replicated, with documented standby initialization/policy requirements. The standby also records its own audit activity. Option C imports Data Guard concepts: file-system replication does not require database standby redo logs for synchronous redo transport. Option D invents a database privilege; the setup uses OS accounts, permissions and SSH authentication. Option E is true: one site can host distinct primary/standby locations for different relationships. One location is not simultaneously both roles in one relationship.

Check a configured location with:

```text
acfsutil repl info /acfsmounts/repl_data
```

Monitor progress, bandwidth and snapshot storage. Identify the replication generation before applying requirements. B/E avoids presenting an invented privilege or an old protocol threshold as verified current behavior. If an instructor insists on three choices, request the intended protocol/version rather than inventing a third current 19c answer.

text: Which three events occur when a node fails in an Oracle Clusterware 19c Cluster? (Choose three.)

options.text: Cluster resources running on the failed node must be recovered when the node is restarted.
Cluster Resources running on the failed node are relocated to one or more surviving hub nodes.
Cluster Resources running on the failed node are suspended until the node is restarted.
Sessions connected to the failed node could be relocated to one or more surviving nodes.
The node is evicted from the cluster.

explanation:
Options B, D and E describe the expected HA response, with qualifications about restartable resources and capable clients. Clusterware changes membership and protects shared-data integrity, then applies placement and restart policies on surviving nodes.

Option A is false as a universal requirement: an HA resource need not wait for the failed node to return. Option B is intended for relocatable resources with a valid surviving placement. A local-only resource or an application with unsatisfied dependencies is not guaranteed to restart elsewhere. Option C is false because resources are not universally suspended until the failed node restarts.

Option D deliberately says could. Clients configured for supported recovery can reconnect or replay work on a surviving instance. This does not mean an arbitrary server process, its memory and its unfinished transaction move unchanged. TAF has recovery limitations; Application Continuity needs suitable configuration and replay-safe workload.

Option E describes removal of a failed member and, where needed, fencing/eviction to prevent split-brain writes. A powered-off server is already unable to write, but membership and recovery consequences remain.

Test a service connection through the service/SCAN address during a node failure. Check server resource placement separately from the client error/replay result. Successful resource restart proves server-side availability, not necessarily preservation of every in-flight business operation. Recovery requires both the cluster's resource management and appropriate application connection behavior.

text: Which statement describes the purpose of colocation_tag for client routing with Oracle database 19c?

options.text: When possible, clients with the same colocation_tag are routed to the same instance that offers a given service.
When possible, clients with the same colocation_tag are routed to the same available instance even if a preferred instance is available.
When possible, clients with the same colocation_tag could be routed across a set of preferred instances based on a specific load balancing option.
When possible, clients with the same colocation_tag are routed to the same available instance when a preferred instance is not available.

explanation:
Option A is correct. COLOCATION_TAG provides best-effort association between a tag and an instance offering the requested service. Related sessions may then share cache locality and reduce inter-instance traffic.

Option B incorrectly invents a rule that bypasses preferred placement in favor of an available instance. A tag does not make a non-offering instance a valid service target. Option C describes spreading a tagged group by load balancing rather than its colocation objective. Option D unnecessarily restricts the feature to the absence of preferred instances. It also applies to ordinary eligible connections.

Example descriptor fragment:

```text
(CONNECT_DATA=
  (SERVICE_NAME=orders.example.com)
  (COLOCATION_TAG=regionalorders))
```

The same tag/service normally maps clients toward the same instance. The words when possible matter: reaching maximum load or changing service membership can change the mapping. It is neither a permanent physical-server binding nor a transaction consistency mechanism.

For example, repeated requests sharing a small working set may benefit from one tag. Giving every client the same tag can concentrate work, so measure locality savings against concentration costs. Confirm where the service runs before diagnosing the tag. Session colocation does not replace service failover configuration or preserve an unfinished transaction when an instance fails. Evaluate the hint alongside service goals, instance capacity and actual global-cache traffic rather than assuming that fewer connection targets always means better performance.

text: Which four statements are true about an Oracle Database RAC software installation? (Choose four.)

Fix-up scripts generated during the installation must be run as root on UNIX platforms.
The software must be installed into a local file system on each node.
The software must be installed into a cluster file system.
RAC installations require Oracle Enterprise Edition.
The software can be installed into an ACFS file system.
The software must be installed on all nodes in the cluster.

There are four true statements in 19c: A, B, E and F. The original Choose three instruction omitted a valid answer; the count has been corrected instead of incorrectly rejecting root prerequisite fixup scripts.

Option A is true: installation-owner SSH equivalence can be configured beforehand. Option B is also true: OUI/CVU prerequisite fixup scripts perform privileged OS changes and run as root, directly or using configured privilege delegation.

Option C is false because local home placement on each selected node is not the only supported arrangement. Option D makes the opposite absolute claim and is false. text: Which two statements are true about initialization parameters for Clustered ASM instances? (Choose two.)

options.text: The maximum value of ASM_POWER_LIMIT is 1024.
The default value of INSTANCE_TYPE is ASM.
A change to ASM_DISKSTRING requires a restart of all ASM instances for the change to take effect.
The ASM_DISKGROUPS parameter is optional.
ASM_POWER_LIMIT controls the number of RDBMS instances that can access a disk group while it is being rebalanced.

explanation:
Options A and D are correct, with a compatibility qualification for A. ASM_POWER_LIMIT sets default rebalance effort, whereas ASM_DISKGROUPS is optional and concerns startup mounting.

Option D is true: ASM_DISKGROUPS is optional, and Clusterware can manage disk-group resources. This does not make every disk discoverable or every group mounted under every configuration. Option E assigns an unrelated purpose: rebalance power changes background effort, not the maximum number of database clients.

A diagnostic session can inspect:

```sql
SHOW PARAMETER asm_power_limit
SHOW PARAMETER asm_diskstring
SHOW PARAMETER asm_diskgroups
```

Measure foreground latency during rebalance. Raising power may shorten maintenance while increasing competition for shared storage. It is not an availability setting or a remedy for mismatched devices. Check the disk-group compatibility before assuming all values up to1024 are operationally usable, and choose the maintenance trade-off from workload measurements.

text: Which three statements are true about undo management in a RAC environment? (Choose three.)

options.text: You can dynamically assign a newly created undo tablespace to an instance.
In a policy-managed RAC database, an undo tablespace may automatically be created if OMF is enabled for the database.
An instance that performs instance recovery can write to the undo tablespace of a failed instance.
A mixture of automatic undo management and manual undo management is supported within a RAC database.
It is necessary to assign a specific undo tablespace to a specific instance.

explanation:
Options A, B and C are correct. Undo generation belongs to an instance, while shared-storage access permits another instance to recover a failed instance's transactions.

Option A is true: dynamically switch an instance to a newly created suitable undo tablespace using UNDO_TABLESPACE. Old undo remains protected while required; the change does not discard active transactions. Option B is true: a policy-managed database with OMF can automatically allocate undo when an instance starts as the server pool grows.

Option C is true with Oracle's qualification: another instance can update an undo tablespace during transaction recovery if no other instance is currently using it for undo generation or recovery. This does not permit two running instances to generate normal transaction undo into the same assigned tablespace.

Option D is false: all RAC instances must use the same undo-management mode. Automatic/manual modes cannot be mixed inside one database. Option E is too absolute: explicit fixed manual assignment is not universal because policy-managed/OMF automation exists.

Inspect assignments with:

```sql
SELECT inst_id, value FROM gv$parameter
WHERE name = 'undo_tablespace';
```

Do not drop an old tablespace merely because the parameter changed. Check active transactions and retention/recovery requirements. The study distinction is instance-specific undo generation versus shared reading for consistency and writing during failure recovery. A PDB's local-undo arrangement adds a container dimension but does not eliminate the need to distinguish generating and recovering instances.

mnemonic.anchor: Undo generation belongs to an instance, while shared-storage access permits another instance to recover a failed instance's transactions.

text: Which four statements are true about Quality of Service Management (QoS)? (Choose four.)

options.text: It can manage database services only if they are defined as UNIFORM services.
It requires Oracle Grid Infrastructure for a Cluster to be installed and Clusterware to be running.
A server pool can be managed by QoS even if it does have database instances running on any server in the pool.
Databases managed by QoS can be administrator managed or policy managed.
It supports multiple databases assigned to the same server pool.

explanation:
Under the actual supplied wording, B, C, D and E are true in 19c. The old three-answer instruction excluded D despite documented support for administrator-managed databases.

Option A is false: UNIFORM-only is too restrictive. QoS can also manage singleton services when the pool maximum size is one. Option B is true: QoS depends on Grid Infrastructure/Clusterware management resources. Option C literally says a pool can be managed when it DOES have database instances running, which is a normal case. The previous explanation silently read does not; that changes the option and must not be used to justify a key.

Option D is true. Administrator-managed deployments support QoS modes and applicable resource controls. They do not gain the policy-managed ability to grow/shrink instance count by resizing a server pool. Option E is true: QoS supports multiple databases sharing the server-pool/physical-resource environment.

Practically, classify workload by service, set measurable response-time objectives and inspect performance-class bottlenecks. Changing CPU shares and adding a server to a pool are different controls, not equally available in every deployment model. If an explanation says QoS always requires policy-managed databases, check both its release and the particular control.

text: Which three statements are true about ASM Cloud File System (ACFS) encryption? (Choose three.)

options.text: A copy of an encrypted file is not encrypted unless it is created in an encrypted directory.
An ACFS snapshot can be ACFS encrypted.
acfsutil encr off can be run by an encryption manager who may not have system administrator privileges.
acfsutil encr on can be used to specify the encryption key length for a directory or file.
acfsutil encr init is used to establish role separation between encryption managers and encryption auditors.

explanation:
A, B and D are supported. C is imprecise:19c allows file owners to decrypt owned paths without system-administrator privilege, but does not define a generic encryption-manager role granting authority over an entire file system. The revised key uses the three choices verifiable without inventing that role.

Option A is true. A copy is a new file whose encryption follows the destination-directory policy, not automatically the source file's status. Option B is true with scope: snapshots preserve encryption, and read-write snapshot files can be encrypted/decrypted/rekeyed by targeting their snapshot paths. A file-system-wide operation does not automatically traverse .ACFS/snaps.

Option C is not an unconditional permission rule: non-root owners can run encr off on owned files/directories; file-system-wide decryption requires administrator privileges. Option D is true: encr on accepts AES/key-length arguments for target files/directories. Option E is false: encr init initializes key storage, not the asserted manager/auditor role separation.

Inspect status explicitly:

```text
acfsutil encr info -m /acfsmounts/acfs1 -r /acfsmounts/acfs1/exports
```

Protect copies and editor-created replacements using encrypted destination directories. If C merely means an appropriately authorized file owner, it can also be true, making this question ambiguous. ACFS encryption is file-system data-at-rest protection; it is not the supported replacement for database encryption of Oracle datafiles.

text: Which three statements are true about the Global Resource Directory (GRD) in Oracle 19c RAC database and in Clustered ASM? (Choose three.)

options.text: Only one GRD shadow resource may exist for an Enqueue Resource.
Shadow GRD resources may exist in more than one database instance for a resource.
Clustered ASM has GRD resources distributed among all ASM instances.
All GRD Enqueue Resource master metadata is held in the large pool of the same database instance.
All GRD Enqueue Resource master metadata is held in the shared pool of the same database instance.
RAC databases have GRD cache resources distributed among all the database instances and stored in the large pool of each instance.
RAC databases have GRD cache resources distributed among all the database instances and stored in the shared pool of each instance.

explanation:
B, C and G are the intended answers, but the detailed master/shadow memory wording is implementation oriented. The reliable broad concept is distributed resource coordination, not a public tuning interface for moving arbitrary GRD structures between memory pools.

Option A is false: multiple instances can need a local representation of a distributed resource. Option B is true: shadows may exist on several instances while a resource master coordinates access. Mastering one resource does not place every resource master in that instance.

Option C reflects clustered ASM's coordinated resource management across participating ASM instances; Flex ASM does not require an ASM instance on every database node. Options D and E wrongly centralize all enqueue-master metadata in one instance. Option F identifies the large pool instead of the intended shared-pool/distributed arrangement in G.

Conceptually, a resource can be mastered by instance 1 and accessed from instances 2 and3. Local participants retain state while distributed services coordinate ownership. Failure leads to membership recovery/remastering; the architecture is not one metadata server whose loss makes every shared object unreadable.

For actual diagnosis, begin with documented global-cache waits and global dynamic views, then investigate workload and interconnect evidence. Do not change hidden parameters or resize the large pool solely because an exam mentions GRD. The precise shared-pool/shadow claims are retained as intended terminology, with their limited direct verification in the public administration sources explicitly stated.

text: Which two statements are true about load balancing using a database service in a RAC environment? (Choose two.)

options.text: Client-side connect time load balancing works only if it uses a tnsnames entry specifying LOAD_BALANCE=yes.
Server-side connect time load balancing is done at the time of the initial connection attempt to the database service.
Server-side load balancing connections are always distributed across instances based on the fastest response time for the service.
Client-side connect time load balancing is done at the time of the initial connection attempt to the database service.
In client-side load balancing, the SCAN listener uses the Load Balancing Advisory to direct a connection request to the least loaded instance hosting the service.

explanation:
Options B and D are correct. Both forms of connect-time balancing act while establishing a connection, but at different decision points: the client chooses a listener address, while server-side balancing helps choose a suitable service instance.

Option A is false because only is too restrictive. An explicit tnsnames.ora LOAD_BALANCE setting is not the sole supported way for capable clients to obtain multiple-address/SCAN balancing. Option B correctly places the server-side decision at initial connection time.

Option C is false: always fastest response time is too narrow. Routing depends on service goals, available handlers and current load information, not a guarantee about future response times. Option D correctly describes the client-side timing. Option E describes a server-side listener decision but calls it client-side; its label is therefore wrong.

For example, the client can select one SCAN address; that listener identifies a suitable service instance and redirects the request to the local listener. Choosing a SCAN listener does not alone select the final database instance. Address reachability and final service placement are different questions.

Also distinguish connect-time decisions from runtime load balancing in a connection pool. A pool may retain physical connections and distribute subsequent requests using service advisories. Changing LOAD_BALANCE in a connect descriptor does not migrate a transaction already executing in an established session or automatically rebalance all currently connected users.

mnemonic.anchor: An explicit tnsnames.ora LOAD_BALANCE setting is not the sole supported way for capable clients to obtain multiple-address/SCAN balancing.

text: Which three statements are true concerning Automatic Database Diagnostic Monitor (ADDM) for RAC? (Choose three.)

options.text: It can analyze performance over any given time period.
It can diagnose skew in response time.
It can analyze performance using data captured on all instances.
It can only analyze performance on the instance running the ADDM job.
It can diagnose latency problems in the Cluster Interconnect.
It runs automatically in Instance ADDM mode after each AWR snapshot is created.

explanation:
Options B, C and E are correct. RAC-aware ADDM uses AWR information to identify database/cluster-level problems, including imbalance that cannot be fully explained by looking at only one instance.

Option A is too broad: analysis requires an interval represented by suitable AWR snapshots, not an arbitrary period without captured information. Short transient incidents diluted across a long snapshot interval may need ASH analysis. Option B is true: response-time/workload skew can expose uneven instance behavior. Option C is true: Database-mode ADDM considers participating instances, while Partial and Instance modes narrow scope.

Option D is false: the instance executing the advisor job does not restrict all analysis to that instance. Option E is true: interconnect latency/global-cache behavior can contribute findings. ADDM does not physically test cables or prove that the network is the only cause of a wait. Option F is false as a blanket RAC rule: automatic database-level analysis must not be described as always Instance-mode ADDM after every snapshot.

For a slowdown, choose snapshots covering the incident and compare cluster-wide findings against individual instances. If one instance contributes most DB time, inspect service/workload placement before merely adding instances. Correlate global-cache findings with interconnect and CPU scheduling measurements. text: Which two statements are true about High Availability NFS (HANFS)? (Choose two.)

options.text: HANFS provides high availability in case of an NFS client failure.
HANFS' performance depends on the characteristics of the underlying ASM disks.
HANFS does not depend on NFS services provided by the underlying operating system.
HANFS provides high availability in case of cluster node failure.
NFS client requests are distributed by DNS in a round-robin fashion to the cluster nodes that export the NFS filesystem.

explanation:
B and D are correct. HANFS makes an NFS export highly available by pairing it with a Highly Available Virtual IP (HAVIP) and registering the export and its dependencies with Clusterware. It protects the server-side service; it does not make every possible client failure disappear.

A is false: a failed NFS client is outside the server failover protection described here. Repairing that client, restoring its network, or restarting its application is a separate concern.
B is true: an ACFS export ultimately uses an ADVM volume and ASM storage. Slow disks, insufficient bandwidth, and storage contention can therefore limit its performance. Availability management does not replace the underlying I/O path.
C is false: Oracle requires a working operating-system NFS server configuration before configuring ACFS NFS exports. The Clusterware agents manage availability around those services.
D is true: when a hosting node fails, the HAVIP and associated export resources can be recovered on an eligible surviving node. Clients continue using the advertised endpoint rather than learning a new server address.
E is false: the availability mechanism is a managed HAVIP/export relationship. It is not defined as DNS round-robin distributing every request among export nodes.

Practical inspection:
```text
srvctl config havip
srvctl status havip
srvctl config exportfs
srvctl status exportfs
```
A useful lab mounts the export through its HAVIP name and compares resource placement before and after a controlled relocation. Observe any client-visible pause separately from eventual resource recovery; server high availability is not a promise of zero latency during every failure.

text: For which three entities can the "what-if" command evaluation be used to determine the impact of clusterware management operations in Oracle 19c Clusterware? (Choose three.)

options.text: Cluster resources
Database transactions
Local resources
Administrator-defined resources
Pluggable Databases (PDBs)

crsctl eval stop resource myapp

text: Which two statements are true concerning the installation of Oracle Grid Infrastructure 19c Cluster? (Choose two.)

options.text: The Grid Infrastructure Management Repository is only required when using ASM.
Specifying the use of Grid Naming Service is optional.
Normal Redundancy ASM Disk Groups used for Clusterware files will contain three voting files regardless of the number of failgroups.

a resource dependency definition
an application resource

explanation:
D is the only universally required choice as this question is worded. Clusterware must have a registered application resource with suitable attributes and an agent to manage. The original request to choose two had no universally valid pair.

A is conditional: Oracle requires a dependent VIP when clients access a failover application through a network and its placement permits it to move between nodes. A non-network batch application does not inherently require its own VIP.
B is not universally required as an explicitly administrator-defined component. Placement can use suitable existing pools and resource attributes; every application does not require creation of a new server pool.
C is conditional. Dependencies should describe real prerequisites such as a filesystem or VIP, but an independent resource need not depend on another application resource.
D is required: the resource definition tells Clusterware what it manages, which agent to use, how to monitor it, and what recovery policy to apply.
E is conditional. The built-in scriptagent is appropriate for shell or batch action scripts. Oracle also provides appagent and supports custom agents; a script agent is not mandatory for every application integration.

A practical design begins by specifying start, stop, check, and cleanup behavior, then adds the actual prerequisites. A network service might depend on both a VIP and ACFS mount, whereas an independent local helper may require neither. Test the selected agent's recovery behavior rather than assuming a VIP by itself makes a process highly available. Resource registration, monitoring, placement, dependency modeling, and network reachability contribute different parts of the solution.
